sens: False and deceptive supernatural deity or power, worshiped in place of the true God
Physical representation of a false deity, object of worship
False god that receives human sacrifices
H7700.detail: 1. The word designates an evil spiritual power, a deceptive supernatural being that people worship believing it to be a god. In Deuteronomy 32:17, the Israelites "sacrificed to idols that are not God": these are not true deities, but deceptive powers. 2. It can also refer to the image or material object to which worship is rendered — the statue or altar where prayers and sacrifices are addressed. 3. An idol receives grave offerings, including human sacrifices: in Psalms 106:37, the fathers of Israel "sacrificed their sons and daughters to idols," which shows the perverse and murderous nature of these cults.
H7700.origine: The Hebrew word shed originally designates a supernatural being, an invisible power. The Greek Septuagint translates it as "demon." It comes from a root that evokes the idea of power or domination. In the Greek Old Testament, it regularly translates the religious phenomenon of false deities against which the prophets warn Israel.
H7700.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Segond, in the two major historical passages where Israel renounces the covenant: in Deuteronomy 32:17, Moses warns that the Israelites "will sacrifice to idols, to new gods," which is infidelity towards the Lord. In Psalms 106:37, the psalmist recalls that the ancestors "sacrificed their sons and daughters to idols," a grave act of apostasy. In both cases, it is the worship of a god other than the Lord, presented as a breach of the covenant and a perversion of worship.
H7700.portee: This word reminds the believer that false gods are not mere human errors or harmless superstitions: they are real and malevolent spiritual powers that lead away from God. Idolatry is not an alternative worship, but a deadly lie that diverts from the truth and leads to abominable acts. Recognizing the true God alone means rejecting these deceptive powers.

sens: Action of causing harm, destroying with force
Brutal behavior that causes damage in society
Oppression and exploitation of the weak
Material destruction, ruin of a city or country
Destructive fury, catastrophe
H7701.detail: 1. Violence is primarily a brutal act that destroys: it ravages cities, overturns homes (Isaiah 51:19 speaks of the devastation and ruin that come together upon Jerusalem). 2. It is also a social sin: those who meditate on ruin in their hearts (Proverbs 24:2), or who hoard in their palaces the products of violence and plunder (Amos 3:10), commit injustice by oppressing others. 3. The Bible designates by this the oppression of the weak: Jeremiah must cry out against violence and oppression because the people suffer (Jeremiah 20:8). 4. Finally, it is the destructive chaos: the Lord warns that it will come like an inevitable plague (Joel 1:15).
H7701.origine: The Hebrew word shod literally designates what overturns, what ravages. It comes from a root expressing the idea of destruction and collapse. It is found in the poetic and prophetic texts of the Old Testament to describe both the damage caused by war or disasters, and the injustices that the powerful commit against the weak. The Septuagint (Greek translation) often renders it with a term meaning "devastation" or "plunder."
H7701.emploi: This word appears 24 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea, Amos) and in Proverbs. The prophets use it to describe social and political chaos: corruption of princes (Ezekiel 45:9), exploitation of the weak (Amos 3:10). In the Psalms and Job, it evokes both material dangers (Psalms 12:6) and human injustices. Isaiah 59:7 places violence in the hands of those who do not know the way of peace. Habakkuk complains about it as a constant spectacle (Habakkuk 1:3). The word thus has several facets: social injustice, war damage, personal cruelty.
H7701.portee: For the believer, recognizing violence as a serious sin helps to see how sin destroys society and affects the innocent. The prophets do not merely describe material ruins: they denounce the injustice of the powerful who oppress the weak. This denunciation invites us to refuse violence in all its forms and to side with the oppressed. It is also a call to build true justice, the kind that only Christ can establish.

sens: To break and crumble the plowed earth with an agricultural tool
To break clods of earth to prepare the soil for sowing
To crumble the ground after plowing
H7702.detail: 1. Harrowing is passing an agricultural tool (the harrow) over a plowed field to break up large clumps of earth and create a fine, smooth surface where seeds can germinate. It is the step that follows plowing: after digging and turning the soil, the farmer harrows to break the compact clods. Isaiah 28:24 describes this action: "Does the one who plows for sowing plow continually? Does he continually open and harrow his ground?" — breaking the ground is to harrow. 2. By extension, harrowing refers to the action of fragmenting and crumbling hard earth. In Hosea 10:11, the prophet uses the image of plowing and harrowing to describe God's disciplinary work: "I will harness Ephraim, Judah will plow, Jacob will harrow" — it is a progressive work of transformation. 3. The word concretely applies to the work of the soil in valleys or open fields, as in Job 39:13 where the author mentions the clods that the harrow or plow breaks in the valleys.
H7702.origine: The Hebrew verb sadad comes from a root that evokes the idea of breaking, fragmenting, dispersing. Its basic image is that of a force that crushes and breaks. In Aramaic and Hebrew, the same root carries this notion of bursting. The word is used in the Piel (intensive form) to emphasize the repeated and vigorous action of harrowing.
H7702.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Old Testament, always in the Piel (intensive form). Isaiah 28:24 uses it in the context of the normal agricultural cycle: the farmer plows and harrows. Job 39:13 refers to the harrowing of the valleys to prepare a fine soil. Hosea 10:11 employs the same vocabulary of plowing and harrowing figuratively, to express God's disciplinary action on His people. In all cases, the word describes a necessary and repeated step in the preparation of the ground.
H7702.portee: This word reminds us that the preparation of a harvest requires regular and methodical work. When Hosea speaks of God who "harrows" Jacob, he evokes a progressive divine discipline, intended to break what is hard and make the people's lives fruitful. For the Christian reader, it is an image of God's patient work in spiritual formation: transformation, crumbling of resistances, preparation of the heart to receive the divine word.

sens: To violently destroy a place, a possession, leaving it to ruin
To pillage, to strip someone or something of its goods
To ravage, to devastate an entire region, like an invading army
To be oneself destroyed, ruined, annihilated
H7703.detail:
1. Devastate primarily means to destroy violently, to reduce to nothing. It is the action of an enemy who invades a house, a city, or a domain and leaves them in ruins. In Proverbs 24:15, one must not devastate the dwelling of the righteous: this means not to ravage it, not to leave it destroyed.

2. The word also describes pillaging, the violent removal of goods: to strip someone of what they possess. In Proverbs 19:26, one who ravages their father deprives him of everything, just as a destroyer takes away the substance of a house.

3. Devastate takes on a massive scope when it refers to the work of conquerors: Jeremiah 4:13 speaks of the destroyer advancing like clouds, and people cry, "We are destroyed!" It is a ravaging of entire regions, fields, and cities.

4. The word is also used to express the final state: to be oneself devastated means to be ruined, annihilated, laid waste. It is the passive form of the verb.
H7703.origine: The Hebrew verb šādad (שָׁדַד) comes from a root that evokes violence and brute force applied to destroy. Its nominal form "devastator" (šōdēd, שֹׁדֵד) designates one who ravages, the aggressor who sows ruin. The word is closely related to the idea of violence, dispossession, and systematic destruction, very common in the narratives of invasions and wars in the Old Testament.
H7703.emploi: This verb appears 47 times in the Old Testament, especially in the writings of the prophets Jeremiah (27 times) and Isaiah, as well as in poetry (Psalms, Proverbs). It describes three types of situations: destruction by an enemy (Jeremiah 4:13, the destroyer advancing), the ravaging of an entire region by an army (Jeremiah 12:12, the devastators on the high places of the desert), and God's judgment on nations (Jeremiah 51:55, the Lord devastates Babylon). Sometimes it is a private crime (ravaging one's father in Proverbs 19:26), more often it is an act of war or the execution of a divine sentence. The participle "devastator" can also refer to a bandit or an aggressor.
H7703.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Bible does not hide the reality of violence, war, and ruin. It shows that God even uses devastation as judgment on sin and injustice: the invaders who ravage the land are sometimes instruments of the Lord. For the reader, it is also a call to protect and not to devastate what does not belong to us, especially the goods of others and the life of a community.

sens: An area of cultivated or cultivable land
An open plain or mountain
H7704A.detail:
1. The word designates an open area of land, cultivated or suitable for cultivation — a field in the sense we know. In Jeremiah 18:14, the prophet speaks of the "fields" of Lebanon to evoke the snow-covered highlands of that mountain, the rocky and exposed surfaces where snow persists and where fresh water springs arise.
2. More broadly, the word can refer to any plain or open surface of mountainous terrain — a cleared area, without thick trees, where rock, snow, or water extends. It contrasts with dense forests.
H7704A.origine: The Hebrew word שָׂדַי (sadi, or "sadai") fundamentally means "field" or "plain." It is closely related to the Aramaic word for "field." In the ancient Greek Old Testament, this name has often been vocalized or associated with other geographical terms: the source definition notes that it is another form or spelling of the name of Mount Hermon (חֶרְמוֹן), Hermon, highlighting that the word applies to the snow-covered highlands of that region.
H7704A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in the context of Jeremiah 18:14. The prophet uses it to speak of the "fields" or high surfaces of Lebanon where the snow of Lebanon never departs — a poetic way of evoking the cold and perennial waters that flow down from this sacred mountain. It is a rare geographical term, deeply rooted in the description of the landscape of ancient Levant.
H7704A.portee: This verse invites the people to meditate on the constancy of nature: the cold springs of Lebanon never run dry, unlike what the unfaithful people have done — they have forsaken the Lord. The image of the snow-covered field where water flows continuously becomes a silent lesson of faithfulness.

sens: A portion of cultivated or arable land
An expanse of soil or terrain
Dry land, as opposed to the sea
A region or country
A surface where vegetation grows
Context or domain of action
H7704B.detail: 1. A field is primarily a parcel of land that is cultivated or could be cultivated: in 2 Samuel 23:11, the Philistines gather near a piece of land filled with lentils, that is, a planted field. 2. The word more broadly designates any expanse of soil, even uncultivated: in 1 Samuel 14:25, the fighters cross a forest over ground where honey flows. 3. It can mean dry land in general, as opposed to the sea — the solid mass on which one walks and lives. 4. By extension, a field can be an entire region or country: the term then covers the whole territory. 5. The word also evokes the surface where life flourishes, where plants grow: in Ezekiel 17:5, a sprout is planted in fertile soil near abundant water, an image of prosperity. 6. Finally, field can designate the context or domain where an action takes place — the scene, the space where something unfolds.
H7704B.origine: The Hebrew word שׂדֶה comes from a root expressing the idea of opening, extending. It originally designates any open and uncovered space, as opposed to built or closed spaces. It is a word deeply rooted in the rural and agricultural life of the ancient Near East: it refers to the concrete reality of the farmer or shepherd who lives off the land. The same root is found in other Hebrew forms related to space and expansion.
H7704B.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the provided usages, always to designate a concrete and precise reality. In 1 Samuel 14:25 and 2 Kings 9:25, it refers to specific lands: a forest with ground covered in honey, a field of Naboth. In 2 Samuel 23:11 and 1 Chronicles 11:13 (two parallel accounts), it is a cultivated piece of land filled with lentils or barley, where the Philistines attempt to invade. In Ezekiel (17:5 and 17:8), the field becomes the backdrop of an agricultural parable: good fertile land with access to water, an image of the favorable context for growth and fruitfulness. The word remains always anchored in the tangible and visible.
H7704B.portee: This word reminds the reader that the action of God and that of man unfold in the material and concrete reality of the world. The field is not an abstract: it is the land that is plowed, seeded, harvested, the soil that nourishes. The images of fertility in Ezekiel invite us to reflect on the conditions that allow for spiritual growth — the water that nourishes, the rich soil, the favorable situation. Recognizing that our lives are rooted in a physical terroir is to accept that faith is lived in the concrete, not in dreams.

sens: Cultivated or cultivable land
Open land without buildings
Real estate, plot of land
Territory, region, country
Space or domain (figurative sense)
H7704G.detail:
1. A field is a plot of land that is cultivated or can be cultivated: in Genesis 2:5, before God made it rain, "no shrub of the field had yet sprung up on the earth," because no one was tilling the ground. It is the land where crops grow and where the earth is worked.
2. By extension, the word designates any open, cleared area of land, without houses or walls: in 1 Samuel 17:44, the "beasts of the field" are the wild animals that live outdoors, away from human dwellings.
3. The field also becomes a property that can be inherited or sold: in Jeremiah 32:8, Jeremiah buys the field of his cousin in Anathoth; in Nehemiah 5:3, people are forced to mortgage their "fields" to survive during the famine.
4. In a broader sense, the field designates a region or territory, opposed to other lands: it is the land of a nation or tribe.
5. The word can take a figurative or symbolic sense to represent a domain of action or a space of influence, although this usage is less frequent in the provided texts.
H7704G.origine: The Hebrew word comes from an ancient root that evokes the idea of an open, cleared space. The Hebrews distinguished between the field (natural and cultivable space) and the city or village (inhabited space). The word has always retained this concrete image of arable land, making it a very common term in the agrarian daily life of Israel.
H7704G.emploi: This word appears 274 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Genesis, Exodus, and Leviticus. It primarily designates the field in the strict sense: tilled land, inherited or purchased property (Genesis 23-25, Jeremiah 32). It can also mean the countryside, the non-urban space where wild beasts live (Genesis 2:19-20, 1 Samuel 17:44). In the laws of Leviticus and Deuteronomy, the field is regulated: sabbatical rest, shared harvest, rights of the poor (Leviticus 19:9, 23:22). The word is finally used to designate an entire country or region (Exodus 9:3, where "the fields" of Egypt are struck by plagues).
H7704G.portee: The field reminds us that the work of the land and subsistence through agriculture were at the heart of life in Israel. For the Christian, this word evokes God's Providence over food (Jesus himself will speak of the fields of the world), and the importance of managing carefully the possessions one has. The laws regarding fields also demonstrate divine justice: leaving gleanings for the poor, respecting the rest of the land—values that challenge the ethical conscience of the reader.

sens: Outdoor working area where fabrics were cleaned and finished
Geographical location identifiable near Jerusalem
H7704H.detail:
1. The word designates a field or area used by fullers (artisans who washed, bleached, and finished fabrics) to dry their cloth in the sun. It was a recognizable workplace in the landscape. In Isaiah 7:3, the prophet is instructed to meet King Ahaz "on the road to the fuller's field," indicating that it was a well-known landmark.
2. This area was located near Jerusalem, close to the aqueduct of the upper pool. In 2 Kings 18:17 and Isaiah 36:2, the Assyrian messengers stop there during the siege of Jerusalem, indicating that it was a strategic and accessible location coming from the north.
H7704H.origine: The Hebrew word שָׂדֶה (sadeh) generally means "field" or "open land." It is formed from a root denoting open, unbuilt space. Here, it is specified by the addition "of the fuller" (כָּבַס, kavass, one who washes)—literally "the field of the washer." Thus, it is a compound place name that identified a specific location by the function of those who worked there.
H7704H.emploi: This expression appears only three times in the Bible, always in relation to the events of the siege of Jerusalem by King Sennacherib of Assyria. It appears in two parallel passages: Isaiah 36:2 and 2 Kings 18:17, which recount the same military campaign with the same details, as well as in Isaiah 7:3, where Isaiah is sent to meet King Ahaz during an earlier threat. The term serves to anchor the divine event in a specific and recognizable place, showing that God acts in the real history of men.
H7704H.portee: This small geographical detail reminds us that the word of God does not descend from heaven in an abstract manner: it meets kings and prophets in concrete locations, at crossroads of history. God intervenes not in an imaginary world, but in the real life of His people, at the heart of political and military crises.

sens: Area of cultivated or cultivable land
Open space, uncovered land
Dry land, as opposed to the sea
The collective of wild animals or plants
H7704I.detail:
1. A field is primarily a defined portion of land intended for cultivation or work: it is the place where what has been sown grows, where one harvests. In Exodus 23:29, the context shows that fields are these open lands where crops are cultivated and where wild beasts also multiply when they are abandoned.
2. The word more broadly designates any uncovered, uninhabited space, contrasting with the village or city: it is the countryside, the wild space. In 2 Kings 4:39, the servant "goes out into the fields" to gather plants, which shows that the field is the free space, far from dwellings.
3. By extension, the field represents dry land, the habitable continent, as opposed to the sea: it is the land that nourishes living creatures.
4. Finally, the word can designate the entirety of wild creation, the beasts and plants that live freely, without domestication: "the beasts of the field" in Jeremiah 12:9 refers to all the wild animals that roam freely.
H7704I.origine: The Hebrew word שָׂדֶה (sadeh) comes from a root meaning "open" or "uncovered," hence the idea of an unbuilt, unfenced space. It belongs to the same family as words designating wide, expansive things, without defined boundaries. In the Greek Septuagint, it is often translated as "agros" (ἀγρός), which has the same meaning of field or cultivated land, and it is the word that New Testament authors adopt.
H7704I.emploi: The word appears in very diverse contexts: fields to cultivate (Exodus 23:29), herbs and wild plants that are gathered there (2 Kings 4:39), but especially wild animals that live there. Most biblical uses of the word sadeh associate fields with wild beasts: in Deuteronomy 7:22, Job 40:15, Jeremiah 12:9, we speak of the "beasts of the field." This is why the Segond sometimes translates the word as "wild" when it refers to uncultivated animals or plants: in 2 Kings 4:39, the wild gourds are not regular crops. The word thus embodies both the place (the uncovered space) and what lives there naturally (wildlife).
H7704I.portee: The field reminds the believer that God reigns over all creation, including what seems untamed or wild. When the Bible mentions the beasts of the field, it emphasizes that nothing escapes divine providence: even the fiercest animals depend on God. This also invites contemplation of the visible creation as the work of the Creator and the place where His power is exercised.

sens: Cultivated land intended for agricultural production
Open space, plain, countryside
Natural territory where wild animals live
Joy and delight of nature
H7704M.detail:
1. The field is primarily a piece of land that is cultivated to yield crops: in Deuteronomy 32:13, Israel eats "the fruits of the fields," which clearly refers to agricultural products derived from the worked earth.
2. The word also designates the open space of the countryside, in contrast to the mountain or the city: in Psalms 80:14, the field is referred to as an accessible and visible area in the landscape.
3. The field is also the natural habitat of wild animals: Isaiah 56:9 calls for "the beasts of the fields" to come, and Psalms 50:11 states that God knows "everything that moves in the fields."
4. Sometimes the word takes on a nuance of joy and delight: Psalms 96:12 asks that "the fields be glad with all that is in them," meaning that the whole earth rejoices.
H7704M.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of a wide and open space. It concretely designates any cleared land, whether cultivated or wild, in contrast to urban or mountainous areas. The word has retained this fundamental meaning of accessible and living territory throughout Scripture.
H7704M.emploi: The word appears about a dozen times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms, the prophet Isaiah, and the book of Lamentations. It is used to speak of the agricultural wealth that Israel receives from God (Deuteronomy 32:13), of creation that depends on God (Psalms 50:11, Psalms 104:11), or of the suffering caused by famine (Lamentations 4:9). In Psalms 96:12 and Joel 2:22, the fields are called to rejoice, a poetic image of the entirety of creation participating in the praise of God.
H7704M.portee: The field reminds the reader that the earth is God's domain: it is from Him that the harvests and the goods necessary for life come. These passages invite us to recognize that our food and prosperity are gifts, not independent acquisitions. They also show that all of creation — the earth, the animals, the countryside — is called to rejoice and glorify God, which elevates the believer's gaze beyond mere material interests.

sens: Woman belonging to the harem of a king or a wealthy man, of lower status than the legitimate wife
Kept woman, companion for pleasure
H7705.detail:
1. The word designates a woman who lives in the royal harem or that of a high-ranking man, such as King Solomon. She does not have the official status of the main wife, but she belongs to the lord who provides for her. In Ecclesiastes 2:8, Solomon lists his wealth and pleasures: he mentions "many women," his concubines, as a mark of his power and oriental luxury.
2. The term more broadly evokes the figure of the woman kept for the pleasure and companionship of the master, without the rights or dignity of a recognized wife. This is an ancient practice in royal courts, attested throughout the ancient Near East.
H7705.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁדָּה (shiddah) has an obscure meaning and its root is not clearly established in the Hebrew language. It appears only once in the Bible. The etymology remains uncertain, but the context and ancient translations (Septuagint, Vulgate) clearly associate it with the notion of concubinage, a common practice in eastern courts.
H7705.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ecclesiastes 2:8, where the Preacher (presented as Solomon) lists all his accumulated wealth and pleasures. He mentions "many women," his concubines, as luxury items acquired in his hedonistic quest. This passage illustrates the material and sensual accumulation that Solomon pursued before concluding that everything is vanity.
H7705.portee: This word reminds us how wealth and power can lead to the objectification of women, treating them as possessions rather than as persons. The ecclesiastical context shows that Solomon himself, at the end of his life, judges this pursuit of vain and unsubstantial pleasures: it is a discreet warning against covetousness and the use of power to satisfy fleeting desires.

sens: The one who possesses absolute power, without limit
The one who exercises sovereign authority over all creation
The one whose thoughts and justice cannot be fathomed
H7706.detail:
1. The Almighty is the one whose power has no limits: He can accomplish what no creature can do. Abraham hears Him say, "I am God Almighty" (Genesis 17:1), as if to affirm that nothing is impossible for God, even a miraculous birth. This power is expressed through works that only God can perform: He gives life and death, He blesses or destroys.
2. This name designates God as the one who reigns with sovereign justice over all that exists. Job acknowledges that the Almighty "does not answer" according to our human criteria, for His justice surpasses our understanding (Job 37:23). We cannot "fathom the thoughts of God, attain the perfect knowledge of the Almighty" (Job 11:7): His wisdom eludes us.
3. Finally, the Almighty is the one in whom we trust beyond what we understand. Naomi changes her name to "Mara" (the Bitter) because "the Almighty has made me bitter" (Ruth 1:20-21): even in suffering, she recognizes that everything comes from His sovereign hand.
H7706.origine: The Hebrew word shaddai likely derives from a root meaning "mountain" or "power" in the ancient languages of the Middle East. It is one of the oldest names for God in the Hebrew Bible, used since the patriarchs. It is related to the notion of irresistible strength that recalls the grandeur of mountains. This distinct name from "Yhwh" (the Eternal) emphasizes a particular aspect of God: His absolute power and ability to accomplish the impossible.
H7706.emploi: This word appears 48 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Genesis (where it affirms God's power towards the patriarchs), in the Book of Job (where it becomes central: more than 30 occurrences), and in the Psalms. In Genesis, God reveals Himself as "the Almighty" before concluding His covenants (Genesis 17:1, 28:3, 35:11). In Job, the word takes on a different tone: the justice of the Almighty is questioned in the face of suffering (Job 11:7, 22:25, 37:23). The meaning remains constant — absolute power — but the relationship varies: assurance with the patriarchs, questioning and trust despite incomprehension with Job. In the prophets, this title reinforces the announcement of divine judgment (Isaiah 13:6, Joel 1:15).
H7706.portee: Calling God "the Almighty" is for the believer a source of unwavering confidence: if nothing escapes His power, no situation is without hope. But this name also invites us to humility: we cannot understand all of God's plans, and it is precisely because He is greater than us that we can entrust our lives to Him, even in doubt or suffering. Job discovers this by renouncing to judge God according to our logic: true faith is to say "You are Almighty" without first demanding to understand.

sens: Father of Elizur, prince of the tribe of Reuben at the time of the Exodus
H7707.detail: Schedéur is a man living during the time of the Exodus from Egypt. He is the father of Elizur, who is named prince (leader) of the tribe of Reuben during the census of the people in the wilderness of Sinai (Numbers 1:5). Elizur bears the title of "prince of the sons of Reuben" and represents his tribe in the various stages of the organization of the camp of Israel: during the census, during the organization of the camps (Numbers 2:10), during the offerings of the princes at the tabernacle (Numbers 7:30-35), and at the departure from the wilderness (Numbers 10:18).
H7707.origine: The name Schedéur means "one who casts light" or "illuminator." It is composed of two Hebrew elements: the first evokes the idea of throwing or projecting, and the second that of light or brightness. It was a common name among the ancient Hebrews, often expressing qualities or blessings.
H7707.emploi: Schedéur appears only five times in the Bible, all in the book of Numbers, and always as the father of Elizur. He is mentioned during the census of the Israelites at Sinai (Numbers 1:5), in the organization of the encampments (Numbers 2:10), during the solemn offerings of the princes of the twelve tribes (Numbers 7:30 and 7:35), and at the time of the departure from the wilderness (Numbers 10:18). Schedéur himself never acts directly in the narratives; he is only identified by his name as a father, which shows the importance of lineage in the genealogical and administrative order of Israel.

sens: Valley south of the Dead Sea, region of the cursed cities
Fertile but dangerous area, rich in mineral deposits
H7708.detail:
1. The valley of Siddim is a region located near the Dead Sea (also called the "Salt Sea"), where the five cities including Sodom and Gomorrah were located. It is there that the kings of these cities confronted the invaders from the North (Genesis 14:3, 14:8).
2. This valley was remarkable for its pits of bitumen, a black and viscous substance that naturally accumulated there. These deposits made it both valuable and dangerous: in fleeing the battle, the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah perished there, falling into these pits (Genesis 14:10). The Hebrew name evokes flat and cultivable land, but here the landscape was marked by these strange mineral riches.
H7708.origine: The Hebrew name Siddim comes from a root meaning "field" or "plain." It designates an open and relatively flat terrain suitable for agriculture. However, this particular valley was geologically unique: located in the depression of the Dead Sea, it contained natural deposits of bitumen, which the Bible expressly mentions. The place embodies the biblical contrast between apparent fertility and the divine judgment that weighs upon the cities of sin.
H7708.emploi: The valley of Siddim appears only three times in the Bible, all in the account of Genesis 14, where it is the scene of the battle between the kings of the five cities and the invading kings from Mesopotamia. It symbolizes the domain of the cursed cities. The account specifies right away that it corresponds to the region of the Salt Sea (Genesis 14:3), an essential location for the reader. The mention of the pits of bitumen distinguishes it from ordinary valleys and underscores its character as a land marked by desolation and judgment.
H7708.portee: The valley of Siddim reminds us that divine judgment falls even on lands coveted by human pride. The detail of the pits of bitumen, far from being a mere geographical backdrop, shows how God uses nature itself to execute His judgment. For the Christian reader, this name is inseparable from the fall of Sodom and Gomorrah, where sin inevitably leads to ruin.

sens: cultivated or to be cultivated land, plot of land
region or territory
productions of the soil, harvest
H7709.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a plot of cultivated or to be cultivated land — a field in the literal sense where one plants and harvests. In Isaiah 37:27, the field represents that fragile and ephemeral grass that quickly dries up, an image of fragility and mortality.
2. It expands in meaning to region, territory, or area: thus in Isaiah 16:8, the "fields" of Heshbon refer to an entire fertile zone around the city.
3. By metaphorical extension, the word also designates what the land produces — the harvest, the grain itself. In Habakkuk 3:17, "the fields will not yield food" means that the lands will bring forth nothing to eat.
4. In biblical figurative language, the field represents human fragility, the vanity of earthly riches, and the helplessness in the face of God's decrees.
H7709.origine: An ancient Semitic root designating what is cultivated and maintained by man. The mentioned variation (sheremah) belongs to the same family of words. It is the common term in biblical Hebrew for arable land, distinct from the house and buildings — the productive field, the space of agricultural work.
H7709.emploi: This word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in poetic and prophetic texts. It is found in contexts of curse or desolation (burned fields of Kidron in 2 Kings 23:4, devastated territories in Isaiah and Jeremiah), of agricultural helplessness (Habakkuk 3:17: drought depriving the fields of harvest), or of geographical description of a fertile region. In Deuteronomy 32:32, the "land" of Gomorrah symbolizes a corrupted land, with poisoned fruits. The word thus carries a strong theological charge: the field is the place where divine blessing or curse is manifested.
H7709.portee: The field reminds the believer that material life depends on God's blessing. Habakkuk 3:17 shows that even without harvest, faith perseveres: "I will rejoice in the Lord." The field thus becomes the concrete symbol of our dependence on God and the vanity of riches that do not last. It is an invitation to seek first the Kingdom of God rather than earthly goods.

sens: Dried and blackened by the intense heat of the sun or hot wind
Withered, reduced to nothing by extreme weather conditions
Figuratively: destroyed, annihilated by an irresistible force
H7710.detail: 1. The word literally designates what has been grilled, charred, or blackened by fire or extreme heat. In the account of Pharaoh's dream, the "burned" ears of corn (Genesis 41:6) are those that have been dried out by the scorching east wind blowing over Egypt — these are not simply golden ears at harvest, but ears ravaged, unusable, reduced to the state of hollow stubble. 2. By extension, the word describes a state of total destruction, emptiness, and sterility. The seven burned ears in the dream symbolize seven years of famine (Genesis 41:27): everything is consumed, emptied, nothing remains. It is less the action of fire than the result: a dry and irreparable ruin.
H7710.origine: The Hebrew verb שׁדף (shadaph) evokes the image of violent drying caused by heat or wind. It belongs to a small family of Hebrew words expressing the idea of rapid and total destruction by natural forces. The word appears mainly in the participle form ("burned," a state form) in the biblical text, to describe a state rather than a one-time action.
H7710.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Bible, all in the same passage: the account of Pharaoh's prophetic dream in Genesis 41. Joseph interprets the seven burned ears as a symbol of the seven years of famine that will ravage Egypt. The context is never one of actual combustion in the strict sense, but always of damage caused by natural elements (the east wind drying) or of symbolic ruin. The word expresses complete uselessness and total loss.
H7710.portee: This word reminds the reader that hunger and destruction do not come by chance, but are inscribed in signs that God gives to His servants so that they may prepare. Joseph, by interpreting the burned ears, shows how divine wisdom allows for anticipating disasters and saving a nation. It is a lesson in vigilance and trust in God's providence that speaks before misfortune arrives.

sens: Dried or withered grain affected by fire or disease
Harvest ruined by a natural calamity
Powerlessness and desolation
H7711A.detail:
1. The word refers to wheat or a harvest that has been consumed, scorched, or dried up — either by fire, a plant disease, or intense drought. In 2 Kings 19:26, the prophet Isaiah describes the Assyrians as 'wheat that dries before the stalk is formed': it is the image of a plant that will never reach maturity.
2. Broadly speaking, it signifies any harvest or crop that has been destroyed and rendered useless, incapable of providing sustenance. The context in 2 Kings 19:26 shows that this burnt wheat symbolizes powerlessness and total destruction — the inhabitants of the kingdom of Israel are compared to plants without strength or utility.
3. Figuratively, the word evokes desolation, inefficacy, and annihilation in the face of God's power: just as burnt wheat cannot nourish anyone, so these men can accomplish nothing.
H7711A.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁדֵפָה (shedéphah) comes from the root שׁדף (shdaf) which means 'to burn', 'to wither', 'to scorch'. It is a variant of שִׁדָּפוֹן (shiddaphôn) which has the same meaning. The underlying image is that of combustion, violent drying that ravages plants and renders them sterile. This word belongs to the vocabulary of agricultural calamities in the Bible.
H7711A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 19:26. In this passage, the king of Assyria boasts of his power and threatens Jerusalem. The prophet Isaiah, reporting the king's words, mocks him by comparing the inhabitants and enemy kingdoms to 'wheat that dries before the stalk is formed' — that is, to something fragile, destined to fail, incapable of resisting the hand of God. It is an image of contempt and absolute powerlessness.
H7711A.portee: This word speaks to us about the fragility of human powers in the face of God. Every empire, every strength, every wealth that claims to oppose God is like burnt wheat — a deceptive appearance, destined for annihilation. For the believer, it is a call not to fear human threats, but to place trust in the one who will bring to nothing all the plans of those who rise against him.

sens: disease of cultivated plants that destroys them
God's punishment that strikes the harvests
H7711B.detail:
1. Rust is a disease that affects crops, particularly grains and other plants. It manifests as drying or transformation that renders the plant unusable. In 1 Kings 8:37 and 2 Chronicles 6:28, rust is mentioned alongside blight as natural plagues that can destroy the harvests of a region.
2. In biblical thought, rust is not a mere agricultural accident: it is a punishment sent by God himself to punish the unfaithfulness of his people. In Deuteronomy 28:22, it is listed among the curses that the Lord inflicts on those who disobey him. Amos 4:9 and Haggai 2:17 present rust as a divine warning: it strikes the harvests to call the people to repentance, 'Yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.'
H7711B.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁדָּפוֹן (shiddaphon) is related to שָׁדַף (shadaph), which means 'to burn' or 'to dry up'. This root evokes the image of intense heat that destroys or consumes. Rust is thus named for the effect of drying and destruction it causes on plants — a true 'burning' of the crops.
H7711B.emploi: The word rust appears five times in the Old Testament, always in the context of curse or divine judgment. It is found in the lists of plagues: in Deuteronomy 28:22 among the diseases and calamities promised to the disobedient; in 1 Kings 8:37 and 2 Chronicles 6:28 in the Temple prayer, listed as one of the crises that God may send; in Amos 4:9 and Haggai 2:17 as an effective punishment that God has already inflicted. Each time, rust symbolizes divine intervention to correct or punish.
H7711B.portee: Rust reminds the believer that God reigns over all creation and that he can use nature as a means of warning. It is an invitation not to neglect calls to repentance, for silence before divine correction becomes guilt. This word also teaches us to see in natural crises, not mere chance, but an opportunity to reflect on our relationship with God.

sens: To make intense efforts to achieve a goal
To struggle determinedly against a difficulty
To seek ardently to accomplish something
H7712.detail:
1. To strive means to exert sustained energy to accomplish something important. It is to show active will, perseverance in the face of an obstacle. In Daniel 6:14, King Darius, learning that Daniel is to be thrown into the lions' den according to his own law, strives all day to find a way to save him — he actively struggles against this fate.
2. The word also evokes the idea of struggling against resistance, wrestling to overcome what opposes us. This struggle can be internal (battling one's own weakness) or external (resisting an imposed constraint).
3. To strive emphasizes perseverance: it is not a sudden effort, but a prolonged, often anxious, effort to achieve one's ends.
H7712.origine: The Hebrew verb שׁדַר (shedar) in the reflexive form (Ithpael) expresses the idea of struggling or turning towards something with eagerness. This grammatical form adds to the simple root the idea of an action that the subject turns towards himself, hence the nuance of 'to strive' rather than simply 'to do'. The root evokes tension, an intention directed towards a goal.
H7712.emploi: This verb appears only once in the preserved biblical text, in Daniel 6:14. It is a key moment in the narrative: King Darius, despite his affection for Daniel and his integrity, finds himself trapped by his own law of the Medes and Persians, which jealous courtiers have manipulated. He strives desperately all day to find a way out, but without success. The context shows a sincere but futile human effort, highlighting man's powerlessness in the face of inflexible laws and God's sovereignty.
H7712.portee: This word reminds the reader of the value of sincere effort and perseverance, even when circumstances seem hopeless. It also shows the limits of human power: the king strives with all his heart, but cannot change the course of events. It is an invitation to seek solutions, not to give up, but also to recognize that only God truly controls the outcome of our struggles.

sens: Line of soldiers aligned side by side
Row of beams or stones in a construction
H7713.detail:
1. A rank is a line of soldiers in formation, each standing next to the other: it is the military order that allows warriors to stand together and fight effectively. In 2 Kings 11:8, the king's guards "will surround the king on all sides, each with weapons in hand" — thus forming a protective rank around him.
2. The word also refers, in construction, to a horizontal row of beams or stones stacked. In 1 Kings 6:9, Solomon covers the temple "with boards and beams of cedar" arranged in regular rows: this is a building technique where each "rank" of wood or stone fits into the levels.
H7713.origine: The Hebrew word סְדֵרָה (sedera) comes from the root שׁדר (seder), which means "to put in order" or "to arrange." This root is found in other Hebrew words expressing order and succession. The basic image is that of an organized sequence, a logical and regular succession — hence "rank" for soldiers and "row" for construction elements.
H7713.emploi: This word appears only four times in the Hebrew Bible. In 1 Kings 6:9, it describes a construction technique of the temple. In 2 Kings 11:8, 11:15, and 2 Chronicles 23:14, it designates the military ranks around Queen Athaliah, who is expelled from the temple: the word evokes the order and discipline of the guards who encircle the king or maintain order in the sanctuary. The context remains each time that of a regular and structured organization.
H7713.portee: Understanding this word helps to imagine how Israel organized its military life and sacred architecture. The "rank" evokes discipline and unity — the strength of one who acts in order rather than in disorder. Through these images of military ranks or rows of wood in the temple, the Bible shows the importance of organization and structure in community life and worship.

sens: Young Jewish man exiled to Babylon, companion of Daniel
He who refused to defile himself by eating the king's food
He who was thrown into the fiery furnace for refusing to bow down to the idol
H7714.detail:
1. Shadrach is a young Jew of noble descent, deported to Babylon during the exile. His Hebrew name was Hananiah ("God has been gracious"), but the chief of the king's eunuchs, Nebuchadnezzar, renamed him Shadrach, a Babylonian name (Daniel 1:7).

2. Along with his companions Daniel, Mishael, and Azariah, he refused to defile himself by eating the king's food and wine, as it would have violated the dietary laws that God had given to the Jews. Despite this disobedience to the king, God blessed them and made them stronger and wiser than all the other young men.

3. Shadrach was among the three friends thrown into a fiery furnace heated seven times more than usual for refusing to bow down to the golden idol erected by Nebuchadnezzar. God intervened miraculously: an angel walked with them in the flames, and they came out without a burn or even the smell of fire on their clothes.
H7714.origine: The Hebrew name Hananiah means "God has been gracious" or "God is gracious." Shadrach is the Babylonian name given to him by the king: it likely means "royal" or "the great scribe," reflecting the status that the sovereign intended to confer upon him by integrating him into his court.
H7714.emploi: Shadrach primarily appears in the book of Daniel, particularly in chapters 1 to 3, which recount the story of four young Jews deported to Babylon during the exile of the kingdom of Judah. He is first presented as one of these young men "without defect, handsome in appearance, well-versed in all wisdom" (Daniel 1:4). With his three companions, he becomes a symbol of faithfulness to God even in the face of royal power and threats of death. His story illustrates how God protects and honors those who remain faithful to Him, even in a foreign land.
H7714.portee: The story of Shadrach encourages believers to remain faithful to their religious convictions, even under pressure or threat. It shows that refusing to compromise with evil is to honor God and receive His blessing and protection. It also teaches that exile or oppression does not separate us from God: He walks with us in trials.

sens: young Jewish man exiled to Babylon during the reign of Nebuchadnezzar
H7715.detail: Shadrach is one of Daniel's three faithful companions, a young Jew from the royal or noble family of Judah, deported to Babylon during the exile. King Nebuchadnezzar renamed him Shadrach (instead of his Hebrew name Hananiah) when he integrated him into the royal court for training (Daniel 3:12). He remained faithful to his faith and the Jewish dietary laws, refusing to defile himself with the king's impure food. Most importantly, when Nebuchadnezzar erected a golden statue and ordered everyone to worship it, Shadrach courageously refused to bow down to this idol, at the risk of his life (Daniel 3:13-14). Thrown into a fiery furnace heated seven times more than usual, he was miraculously saved by God's angel, which led the king to acknowledge the power of the God of Israel (Daniel 3:26-28).
H7715.origine: His original Hebrew name is Hananiah (חֲנַנְיָה), which means "God has been gracious." The Aramaic name Shadrach, by which he was renamed in Babylon, means "royal" or "the great scribe," reflecting the status the king gave him at court. This name change symbolizes the pagan power's attempt to assimilate the exiled young Jews into Babylonian culture.
H7715.emploi: Shadrach appears thirteen times in the book of Daniel, primarily concentrated in chapter 3. Daniel first mentions him in chapter 2 verse 49 when he asks the king to place Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in positions of authority in Babylon. But Shadrach becomes a central character in chapter 3, where the conflict with the king reaches its peak: Shadrach and his companions are denounced for refusing to worship the golden statue (3:12), questioned by the king himself (3:13-14), condemned and thrown into the fire (3:19-23), and then miraculously saved (3:26). The account concludes by showing how the king now proclaims a decree protecting the God of Shadrach (3:28-29).
H7715.portee: The story of Shadrach speaks to every believer faced with choices between obeying God or obeying human authorities. A young man far from his homeland, in a hostile and seductive environment, Shadrach chose to remain faithful to his conscience and faith, even at a cost. His courage reminds us that God honors those who put Him first, and that His protection extends even in the most terrible trials. He is a model of faithfulness and trust in God amid persecution.

sens: domestic animal of the flock, young sheep or young goat
adult ewe or sheep
ram or male goat
victim offered in sacrifice
image of the innocent or the vulnerable
H7716.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the young animal of the flock, a small sheep or a small goat at the time it begins to be raised. This is how Abraham seeks a lamb to offer as a sacrifice (Genesis 22:7), and how the law establishes lambs for the redemption of the firstborn (Exodus 13:13).
2. It also applies to the adult ewe, to the sheep of the flock. When locusts invade the land, they destroy the ewes (Judges 6:4), and the cultivated mountains will be trampled by the wild ewe (Isaiah 7:25).
3. The word also encompasses the ram or the male goat of the flock. The law prescribes a lamb or a ewe among the clean animals (Deuteronomy 14:4).
4. As a sacrificial victim, the lamb occupies a central place: offered at Passover (Exodus 12:3-5), it represents the atonement for sin (Leviticus 5:7).
5. Figuratively, the lamb becomes the image of the innocent who suffers defenselessly, an image that the prophet Isaiah applies to the suffering servant (Isaiah 53:7), and that Jesus himself assumes.
H7716.origine: The Hebrew word seh comes from a root meaning "small" or "young." It designates the young and fragile animal of the flock. The flock in Israel included sheep and goats, often raised together. The word applies to all the young of this flock, or to the flock itself as a whole. This simple and common term reflects the importance of pastoral farming in the life of Israel.
H7716.emploi: The word appears 39 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Pentateuch and the prophets. It occurs in three major contexts: first, civil and religious law (redemption of the firstborn, laws on property and livestock theft), then sacrificial worship (Passover, expiatory sacrifices), and finally the images of the prophet — notably in Isaiah, who sees in the defenseless lamb the image of the suffering just. The meaning of the word does not vary much: it is always the animal of the flock, young or adult, but the usage shifts from the concrete (the real animal of the shepherd) to the symbolic (the lamb as a figure of Christ).
H7716.portee: For the believer, the lamb is much more than a domestic animal: it is the biblical symbol of delivered innocence and redemptive sacrifice. Jesus Christ himself is called "the Lamb of God" — he recapitulates all the lambs of the Old Covenant in his own sacrifice for the salvation of the world. Meditating on this word invites contemplation of both God's sacrificial love and the call to a life of gentleness and innocence.

sens: person who sees an event and can speak about it
person who attests to the truth or innocence of someone
one who stands by someone to support or uphold them
H7717.detail: 1. The witness is one who has seen something with their own eyes and can report it: this is the most direct sense of the word. 2. In a context of justice or conflict, the witness becomes one who will speak to establish the truth and defend the innocent — exactly the role that Job assigns to God when he says "my witness is in heaven" (Job 16:19). God, who sees everything, can attest that Job is innocent despite the accusations of his companions. 3. The word also evokes one who stands beside you, who knows your heart and your life, and who can take your defense. This is why Job appeals to God as a witness: not only does he know everything, but he is capable of intervening to support the one who suffers unjustly.
H7717.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to be present" or "to stand beside." A witness is literally one who is there, who has seen, and who shares what they have observed. This notion of presence and direct knowledge is at the heart of the Hebrew word.
H7717.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the cry of Job who suffers unjustly. Job invokes God as the only witness capable of certifying his innocence in the face of his friends' misunderstanding. It is an emotional appeal to the one who sees what men do not see, and who can intervene to restore justice.
H7717.portee: This word reminds us that God sees everything we endure in silence and unjustly. Even when no one believes us or understands us, God is the ultimate witness of our heart, our faithfulness, and our innocence. He does not leave us without support: he knows our entire story and can intervene for us. It is a promise of divine defense against injustice.

sens: precious stone of dark and shiny color
stone used in the priestly garments of worship
noble material symbolizing divine wealth and splendor
H7718.detail:
1. The onyx is a precious stone of beautiful appearance, hard and shiny, usually dark in color. It was found in ancient Arabia, mixed with the pure gold of the land of Havilah (Genesis 2:12), and was among the most precious materials available.

2. God commanded that two onyx stones be engraved with the names of the twelve sons of Israel and set on the shoulder pieces of the high priest's ephod (Exodus 28:9): this stone became an integral part of the most sacred liturgical garment. It was also included in the breastplate, placed alongside other precious stones like chrysolite and jasper (Exodus 28:20).

3. The onyx symbolizes heavenly and divine wealth: Job asserts that no earthly wealth can compare to it (Job 28:16), and Ezekiel describes the jewels of Eden, or those of the king of Tyre, as adorned with onyx, an image of glory and superhuman perfection (Ezekiel 28:13).
H7718.origine: The Hebrew word shoham likely designates true onyx, a variety of chalcedony, although the ancients also applied this name to other precious stones like chrysoprase, beryl, or malachite. The exact root remains obscure in biblical texts, but the word belonged to the vocabulary of precious stones in the ancient Near East. The word reflects the importance that the Hebrews placed on luxury materials intended for divine worship.
H7718.emploi: The word onyx appears eleven times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in Exodus and associated books (instructions on the sanctuary and priestly garments), as well as in wisdom and prophetic passages. In Exodus (chapters 25, 28, 35, 39), the onyx is always among the luxury materials that God commands to adorn the sanctuary and the priest's costume: it is a liturgical ornament stone, never ordinary. In Job 28 and Ezekiel 28, the onyx becomes a symbol of immeasurable wealth, beyond the reach of human money. In 1 Chronicles 29:2, King David gathers it for the building of the Temple, associating this stone with the magnificence of worship rendered to God.
H7718.portee: The onyx reminds the believer that the worship rendered to God deserves the best and most costly we have. By adorning the garment of the high priest, this stone signified that one who approaches God on behalf of the people must reflect divine splendor and holiness. For the modern reader, the onyx invites us not to reduce our relationship with God to ordinary or accessory things: it calls for a reverent and magnificent worship.

sens: Name of a Levite from the tribe of Merari
Son of Jaaziah, brother of Beno, Zaccur, and Ibri
H7719.detail: Schoham is a man from the tribe of Levi, a member of the Merarite group (descendants of Merari, son of Levi). He appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 24:27, where he is presented as one of the sons of Jaaziah. Along with his brothers Beno, Zaccur, and Ibri, he is listed among the Levites involved in temple service during the time of the divided monarchy.
H7719.origine: The name Schoham literally means "onyx" in Hebrew, referring to the precious stone. It is a descriptive or symbolic name, common in biblical genealogies where names often evoke a quality or resource. Although this Schoham is mentioned only once, his inclusion in the genealogical record of the temple Levites attests to the importance of families involved in cultic service in Israel.
H7719.emploi: Schoham appears only in 1 Chronicles 24:27, a passage that lists the descendants of Merari designated for service in the temple. This verse lists the children of Jaaziah: Schoham, Zaccur, and Ibri (as well as Beno, mentioned separately). This genealogy belongs to the record of Levitical families established under the reign of David to organize temple worship. The mention of Schoham illustrates the religious administrative structure of Israel and the responsibility of the Merarites in maintaining the tabernacle and the temple.

sens: Crescent-shaped object, worn as adornment or ornament
Pendant or luxury jewelry, often made of gold
Prestigious accessory of kings and warriors
H7720.detail:
1. A crescent is an object shaped like a waxing moon, or more generally a curved shape reminiscent of this lunar phase. In the three biblical passages, it always refers to an ornament: on the necks of the camels of the kings of Midian (Judges 8:21, 8:26), where these crescents shine like pieces of prestige, or on the feet of the women of Jerusalem as luxury jewelry (Isaiah 3:18).
2. The crescents mentioned on the royal camels of Midian are precious pendants, often made of gold or noble metal. Gideon takes them as plunder after his victory (Judges 8:21), alongside gold rings and purple garments, which shows their great value.
3. These objects symbolize the wealth and power of the kings of Midian. Their presence on prestigious animals and on high-ranking women indicates that they serve to display the dignity, status, and prosperity of the wearer.
H7720.origine: The Hebrew word שַׂהֲרוֹן (saharon) comes from the root שׁהַר (sahar), which means "moon" or "to shine like the moon." The crescent, a characteristic shape of the waxing or waning moon, naturally gave its name to any object or ornament having this curved shape. The moon, a symbol of clarity and beauty in the ancient Near East, made these jewels particularly prized.
H7720.emploi: The word appears exactly three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to designate ornaments. Two occurrences are found in the account of Gideon (Judges 8:21 and 8:26): they refer to the gold crescents that Gideon seized as plunder from the camels of the defeated kings of Midian, highlighting their military and economic importance. The third occurrence (Isaiah 3:18) mentions them among the luxurious feminine adornments that God will take away from the haughty women of Jerusalem, grouping them with ankle bracelets and headbands: here, the crescent represents pride and ostentation. In all cases, they are objects of value and prestige.
H7720.portee: These crescents remind us that material wealth and sumptuous ornaments attract attention and flatter pride, but remain things that God can take away or denounce. For the Christian, this word invites reflection on the relationship to beauty and wealth: admiring the splendor of creation is good, but making them idols or sources of pride is dangerous.

sens: Hidden trap or scheme to surprise and harm
Hidden danger that threatens without being seen
Sneaky attack from an enemy
H7722A.detail:
1. This word refers to a hidden trap or scheme set for someone to capture or harm them — like a hunter who sets a concealed trap. In Psalm 35:17, the psalmist prays to God to protect his soul from the snares of his enemies: it is not an open attack, but traps laid in secret.
2. More broadly, it is any hidden danger that threatens without being seen — a silent and invisible threat. The word suggests the idea of devastation and destruction approaching quietly.
3. An ambush is primarily the weapon of the weak or cowardly: instead of confronting openly, one seeks to trap, surprise, and destroy through cunning.
H7722A.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of destruction and devastation. It belongs to a family of terms that describe a danger that unfolds or extends — like ruin that silently spreads. The context of Psalm 35 (a psalm of protest against enemies) shows that it particularly designates organized and hidden malice, that of adversaries who conspire.
H7722A.emploi: This word appears only once in the usages of Psalm 35:17, a psalm where the poet complains about false witnesses who have raised unjust accusations against him. Here, the ambush is the weapon of these wicked enemies: they do not fight face to face, but lay traps. The psalmist asks God to protect his soul and life — that is, his entire being — from these hidden threats. The context shows that the ambush is associated with deliberate malice and the destruction that enemies seek to accomplish in secret.
H7722A.portee: This word reminds the believer that the enemies of God and His people do not always fight openly, but often seek to destroy through cunning and secrecy. It is a call to vigilance and trust in God to be protected from these invisible threats. The psalmist teaches us to cry out to God, not in resignation, but with assurance that our Protector sees what is hidden.

sens: destruction, annihilation of a thing or place
devastation of land, abandonment, desolation
storm, whirlwind, sudden catastrophe
death, disappearance, loss
H7722B.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes destruction and complete annihilation — what remains when something is completely ravaged. In Job 30:3, the miserable flee to places that are "abandoned and desolate": this is the result of the total ruin of a region.
2. It particularly evokes the devastation of lands and fields, their abandonment to sterile solitude. Job 38:27 speaks of making grass sprout in "solitary and arid" places — spaces that no one cultivates anymore, where death reigns.
3. The word also applies to sudden catastrophes that strike like a storm or an irresistible whirlwind. Proverbs 1:27 describes terror seizing "like a storm" and calamity enveloping "like a whirlwind" — the image is that of a destructive force that overwhelms you.
4. Finally, it can mean death or disappearance: in Psalms 63:10, those who seek to "take away" life go toward death — the word expresses here the annihilation of life itself.
H7722B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root evoking a cry, noise, and the idea of rupture or fracture. The basic image is that of something collapsing, breaking, shattering with a violent noise — hence the concrete sense of "noisy destruction." The word belongs to the family of terms describing natural disasters or misfortunes that strike suddenly and completely.
H7722B.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the poetic and prophetic books: Job (3 times), Psalms (2 times), Proverbs (2 times), Isaiah (2 times), Ezekiel and Zephaniah (once each). It designates sometimes the material and concrete ruin of a region (Job 30:3), sometimes the desolation that results (Job 38:27), sometimes a sudden and violent catastrophe (Proverbs 1:27). Its meaning varies slightly according to the context, but always retains the idea of complete and irreparable destruction.
H7722B.portee: This word reminds us that complete destruction is a formidable reality in the world, and it can be the result of God's judgment on evil. But at the same time, the texts that use it show that God controls this ruin and that His justice is exercised against those who do evil. The Christian sees it as a call to take seriously the consequences of sin and to seek refuge in God rather than live in rebellion that leads to destruction.

sens: That which is devoid of meaning, valueless or unfounded
That which is deceitful, contrary to truth
That which is misleading or illusory
That which is vain, useless, without effect
H7723G.detail: 1. Falsehood primarily denotes emptiness, nothingness, that which has no real substance. This is why it is applied to unfounded visions: the false prophets of Ezekiel pronounce "vain" divinations, words that rest on nothing (Ezekiel 13:7). 2. It then signifies a deliberate lie, a word contrary to the truth. This is the false testimony forbidden by the Law (Exodus 23:1), or the "falsehoods" that men say to one another (Psalms 12:3). 3. Falsehood can also be a deception, something that presents itself as true but disappoints: an empty promise, a promise that does not hold. 4. It finally designates the vain, ineffective character of one who relies on empty things (Isaiah 59:4).
H7723G.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁוְא comes from a root evoking emptiness, nothingness. It is akin to the image of the wind that passes and leaves nothing behind. It is the opposite of solidity, truth, and reliability. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this word is often rendered by terms expressing vanity, lies, and that which is unfounded.
H7723G.emploi: This word appears 25 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms, the Prophets, and Proverbs. It primarily describes lies: false testimony (Exodus 23:1), the deceitful words spoken without fear of God. It also characterizes the false prophets who claim to speak for God but only convey their own vain visions, notably in Ezekiel (13:6-9, 21:28). The word can finally qualify that which is futile or without moral value: one who trusts in vain things rather than in the Lord (Isaiah 5:18, Hosea 10:4).
H7723G.portee: This word reminds the believer of the danger of lies and duplicity. Falsehood has no substance; it always collapses. In contrast, the truth of God and His Word are solid and enduring. Recognizing what is false helps the Christian distinguish true prophets from false ones, true promises from illusions, and to live in integrity rather than deception.

sens: That which is empty, hollow, without substance
That which is false, deceitful, devoid of truth
That which is useless, without effect or result
That which is futile, without value or importance
That which is spoken lightly, without respect or commitment
H7723H.detail:
1. The word first evokes emptiness, nothingness, the absence of content: something that has no solid reality. In Psalms 127:1, building a house "in vain" means that the work amounts to nothing, remains sterile and void of fruit.
2. It is also falsehood and lies: to speak "in vain" of the name of God (Exodus 20:7) means to pronounce it insincerely, disloyally or deceptively, or to invoke it to swear falsely.
3. The word denotes uselessness, the absence of result: "in vain have I struck your children" (Jeremiah 2:30) means that the punishment has served no purpose, has produced no correction.
4. It is futility, that which has no real weight or lasting importance: "Turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things" (Psalms 119:37) speaks of everything that distracts from the true, that which is merely a passing distraction.
5. It is also the lack of seriousness and respect: taking the name of God "in vain" (Deuteronomy 5:11) means treating it without reverence, putting it on the lips lightly.
H7723H.origine: The Hebrew root šāvaʿ fundamentally means "to be empty, hollow." It belongs to a family of words that all express absence, nothingness, or insufficiency. The Hebrew term shav is very close to the Greek idea of "kenós" (empty), although the two words have slightly different nuances: shav emphasizes more the uselessness and moral or spiritual vacuity.
H7723H.emploi: The word appears 23 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in the Psalms, Jeremiah, and Job. It designates sometimes the uselessness of human efforts without God's help (Psalms 127), sometimes falsehood and perjury (Exodus 20:7, Psalms 139:20), sometimes the ineffectiveness of punishment (Jeremiah 2:30). Its usage fluctuates: sometimes it qualifies a vain action, sometimes a deceitful statement, sometimes an empty promise. In the context of the name of God, it carries a strong religious charge: it is a serious failure to respect due to the Lord. Job uses it to describe the emptiness of days and human efforts in the face of suffering.
H7723H.portee: This word invites the believer to reflect on what truly matters. Taking the name of God in vain is not just a bad word: it is lacking sincerity before the One who searches hearts. The passages on the futility of works without God (Psalms 127) remind us that our efforts, without His blessing, remain empty. It is also a call to vigilance: not to let our eyes and thoughts focus on what is vain and unfounded.

sens: Member of the tribe of Judah
Son of Caleb and Maacah
Father of Machbenah and Gibeah
H7724G.detail: 1. Sheva is a man from the tribe of Judah, belonging to the lineage of the descendants of Hezron (1 Chronicles 2:49). 2. He is the son of Caleb and his concubine Maacah; he has several half-brothers, including Hur, Shobab, and Ardon, from Caleb's other unions (1 Chronicles 2:49). 3. He is the father of Machbenah and Gibeah, thus continuing the genealogy of Caleb in the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:49).
H7724G.origine: The name Sheva means "the Lord contends" or "the Lord disputes": it evokes the divine action of taking sides, defending one's cause. It is a theophoric name, composed of an element referring to God and an action verb. It reflects the Hebrew practice of naming children in relation to the circumstances or spiritual convictions of the parents.
H7724G.emploi: Sheva is mentioned only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 2:49, in the detailed genealogy of Caleb. He appears in the context of the descendants of Hezron, listed to establish the tribal lineages of Judah. His only biblical mention places him among the ancestors of the Judean families, without any specific account of his deeds or role in the history of Israel.

sens: Man living during the time of the united monarchy in Israel
H7724H.detail: Shesha is an administrative figure during the time of King David and Solomon. He served as a royal secretary (or scribe), an important role that involved managing official documents and correspondence of the kingdom. He is a man whose name appears in several variants in the texts: he is called Shesha in 2 Samuel 20:25, but also Shavsha in 1 Chronicles 18:16 and Shisha in 1 Kings 4:3 — different names likely designating the same person across textual traditions.
H7724H.origine: The name means "Jehovah contends" or "Jehovah disputes". It belongs to the Hebrew naming tradition where the name of God (Jehovah) is combined with a verb indicating an action or quality. This type of theophoric name was common among high-ranking Israelites and expressed a trust in God's action.
H7724H.emploi: Shesha appears only once in the Bible with this specific name, in 2 Samuel 20:25, where he is mentioned as the king's secretary alongside Zadok and Abiathar who served as priests. However, it is very likely that this character is the same Shavsha (1 Chronicles 18:16) and the same Shisha (1 Kings 4:3), under variations of transcription. These variations reflect the diverse transmission of proper names in ancient biblical texts. His role demonstrates the importance of written administration in the royal governance of Israel.

sens: Go back to a place one has left, return physically
Turn away, flee, retreat from something
Bring something or someone back to its starting point, restore it
Turn away from God, abandon Him
Turn back to God again, repent
Reverse a situation, annul or undo what has been done
H7725G.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical movement: returning to a place from which one has departed. Genesis 3:19 speaks of returning to the ground from which man was taken. David and his men return to the land of the Philistines in 1 Samuel 29:11.
2. To retreat or flee from an enemy or threat: the enemies of the psalmist retreat when he cries out to God (Psalms 56:10).
3. To bring back means to bring something or someone to its starting point, to restore it. In Genesis 14:16, Abram brings back Lot and his goods.
4. To turn away from God: to apostatize, abandon Him, and follow other spiritual paths — this is the opposite of faithfulness.
5. To turn back to God after having left Him: this is repentance, a radical change of direction. Jeremiah 31:21 calls Israel to return to the cities that are theirs.
6. To reverse or annul: to undo a decision, withdraw a promise made, or change the course of events.
H7725G.origine: The verb שׁוּב (shuv) comes from a root meaning fundamentally "to turn," "to turn back." It is a very frequent verb in biblical Hebrew, with both concrete and spiritual meanings. The same root is used in its simple forms to express the physical return of a person or thing, and in its intensive forms to express restoration or a change of spiritual direction. It is a word that traverses the entire history of Israel.
H7725G.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible (over 500 occurrences). It first appears in the narratives of Genesis, where the patriarchs regularly return to their homes or are commanded to come back. Throughout the Exodus and the history of Israel, it takes on major spiritual significance: returning to God becomes synonymous with repentance and conversion. The prophets, notably Jeremiah, constantly use it to call the people to turn away from idolatry and turn back to the Lord. Its usage depends on grammatical forms: to return (Qal simple), to bring back or restore (causative forms). The notion of return is central to the biblical message: the Lord Himself is presented as the one who brings back, restores, and forgives those who repent.
H7725G.portee: This word teaches the believer that returning to God is always possible, even after having strayed away. It emphasizes that repentance is not an abstract moral decision, but a concrete change of direction, as real as turning around on a road. It also reveals the divine action: God brings back, restores, and forgives those who return. It is a word of hope that structures the prophetic announcement and the promise of Covenant.

sens: To turn back, to return to a place
To bring something or someone back to their starting point or to their owner
To restore, to return to a previous state
To turn the heart, the soul towards God; to repent
To come back from, to stray from, to abandon a path or an attitude
To bring back, to bring something to mind
H7725H.detail:
1. To return primarily means to turn back and regain a place that one has left: "You are the Lord, my God; restore me, and I will return" (Jeremiah 31:18), where Ephraim asks to be brought back to God, an image of physical return applied to the heart.
2. To bring back refers to the action of making someone or something return, to restore it to its master or its place: "Return the garment you took as a pledge" (Deuteronomy 24:13 conveys the idea of giving back).
3. To restore means to return something to its former state, to repair, to strengthen: "This child will restore your soul" (Ruth 4:15) means that he will give life and hope back.
4. To repent means to turn one's heart towards God, to cease straying from Him: the word expresses less guilt than a true change of direction of the heart.
5. To divert means to cause to cease or to stray: "to divert your captivity" (Lamentations 2:14) means to make it leave.
6. To bring to mind means to recall, to evoke: the heart returns to something it had turned away from.
H7725H.origine: The Hebrew word שׁוּב (shuv) is a very ancient verb, probably related to the physical idea of turning or making a U-turn. It appears in many contexts and combines with other verbs to nuance its meaning: thus "to return" + an action verb creates the idea of "doing again." It is one of the most frequent verbs in the Hebrew Bible, as it expresses the central theological idea of repentance and returning to God, particularly in the prophets.
H7725H.emploi: This verb appears more than a hundred times in the Old Testament and has very varied meanings depending on the context. In the physical sense, it describes returning to a place: "the untrained calf" that Judah asks to be brought back (Jeremiah 31:18). In the legal and social sense, it means to give back or restore: a deposit (Leviticus 5:23), a pledge (Deuteronomy 24:13), or a prisoner (Genesis 40:13 where the chief cupbearer "will be restored"). Theologically and spiritually, it becomes central in the prophetic message: returning to God, repenting, abandoning idolatry (Jeremiah 15:19). The word also expresses the restoration of lands, the temple, the entire nation after exile. It is a key word in Deuteronomy and Jeremiah, where the repentance of the people and the return of the Lord to His people define hope.
H7725H.portee: For the believer, this word opens a perspective of hope: it is never too late to turn to God, to return from one's wanderings. It reminds us that repentance is not primarily a feeling of guilt, but a change of direction, an active return to the Lord. It is also a promise: God Himself "returns" to His people, restores and lifts them up. This word speaks of regained grace.

sens: To go again to a place one has left, to turn back
To divert, to distance (anger, a feeling)
To turn away from something, to abandon it, to renounce it
To turn towards something, to return to it (in a spiritual sense)
To restore, to return to a previous state
To give back, to restore, to repay
H7725I.detail:
1. To return means to go again to a place where one has been, or simply to turn back. When Naomi says to Ruth, "return with me" (Ruth 1:16), she invites her to go back to the land. This is the simplest physical movement of the word.

2. To divert anger or fury means to distance it from oneself, to cause it to cease or to redirect it. When we pray that "the anger of the Lord be diverted" (2 Chronicles 29:10), we ask that this anger does not strike the people but focuses elsewhere or calms down.

3. To turn away from a path or a wrongdoing means to abandon it, to renounce it definitively. Jeremiah reproaches the people for not returning from their wickedness (Jeremiah 23:22): they must abandon evil.

4. To return to God means to turn back to Him after having left or abandoned Him; this is what we call repentance. The prophet urges to "return from his evil way" to draw closer to God.

5. To restore means to bring back to a good or former state. When God "restores" the soul (Psalms 23:3), He puts it back in good condition, He repairs it.

6. To give back or restore means to return what one has received or what one owes. This can be a restitution, a payment, or a reward.
H7725I.origine: The Hebrew verb shuv expresses the fundamental idea of turning, of changing direction. The root evokes the movement of one who makes a U-turn. This word is among the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible, as it describes both the physical movement (returning from a journey) and the spiritual movement (turning towards God or straying from Him).
