It becomes especially famous as the site of the confrontation between David and Goliath, where Saul camped against the Philistines (1 Samuel 17:1). Finally, it is mentioned as a prosperous administrative center under Solomonic rule, demonstrating its economic and political importance throughout biblical history.

sens: mountain city in the territory of Judah
H7755H.detail: Soco is a city located in the mountainous region of southern Judah. It appears only once in the Bible, in the list of cities that Joshua assigns to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of the land. Its location in the mountains of Judah suggests that it was a locality in the hinterland, far from the coast, forming part of the network of fortified cities or settlements that the people of Israel had appropriated.
H7755H.origine: The name Soco literally means "bushy" in Hebrew, an image that evokes the landscape of thickets and dense vegetation in this mountainous region of Judah. This type of geography is found in many Judean localities, where the hills are covered with bushes and sparse vegetation.
H7755H.emploi: Soco is mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in Joshua 15:48, where it is listed among the mountain cities (or "mountains") assigned to Judah during the division of the land of Canaan after the conquest. This brief mention suggests that Soco was a minor locality in terms of political or religious importance, but well established enough to be counted among the official possessions of the tribe.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once during the divided monarchy
Fortified city in the lowlands of Judah
Fortified city in the mountainous region of Judah
H7755I.detail:
1. Soco is a man belonging to the tribe of Judah, son of Heber, mentioned only once in the Bible in 1 Chronicles 4:18 in a genealogy. Little is known about him, except that he descends from a mixed lineage since his mother was Bithiah, daughter of Pharaoh.
2. A fortified city in the lowlands of Judah, cited among the strongholds that King Rehoboam built or strengthened to defend the kingdom (2 Chronicles 11:7).
3. Another city of the same name was located in the mountainous region of Judah. It was taken by the Philistines during an invasion in the time of King Ahaz (2 Chronicles 28:18), demonstrating its strategic importance.
H7755I.origine: The name means "bushy" or "covered with thickets" in Hebrew, evoking a place planted with dense vegetation. This may be a topographical description of the landscape. The same root applies to several places in Canaan, suggesting that multiple locations bore this descriptive name.
H7755I.emploi: Soco appears three times in Chronicles. First as a man in a genealogy from the time of the divided monarchy (1 Chronicles 4:18). Then, the name designates one or two fortified cities of the southern kingdom. One of them is among the cities that King Rehoboam fortified (2 Chronicles 11:7) to strengthen the defense of Judah. The other was occupied by the Philistines during their invasion under King Ahaz (2 Chronicles 28:18), proof that these strongholds were not always able to withstand external threats.

sens: Family of scribes living in Jaebets and descending from Judah through Caleb
H7756.detail: The Sukathites are a family of scribes mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the families of scribes established in Jaebets are listed. According to the text of 1 Chronicles 2:55, they are part of the descendants of Judah, linked to Caleb. The passage places them alongside other families of scribes and indicates that these groups are descended from the Kenites, descendants of Hamath, father of the house of Rechab, a lineage known for its devotion to God.
H7756.origine: The name "Sukathites" likely comes from a Semitic root meaning "bushes" or "thicket" (in Hebrew, סוּכָה sukha), which may have earned them the nickname "men of the bushes." Their connection to the house of Rechab and the Kenites suggests that they were itinerant artisans or specialized scribes associated with this community of trade.
H7756.emploi: The Sukathites appear only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:55. They are listed among the families of scribes living in Jaebets, alongside the Tirathites and the Shimeathites. The genealogical context shows that these three families, although living in Judea, descended from the Kenites, indicating that they formed specialized professional groups, likely tasked with preserving and transmitting written knowledge in the community of Israel.

sens: Edge or hem of a garment, especially at its bottom
Extension of the garment that trails or extends to the ground
Image of majesty and power (referring to God or a king)
Symbol of a person's honor and dignity
H7757.detail:
1. The hem refers to the lower edge of a garment, particularly an ornate one. In the high priest's garment, the hem was adorned with pomegranates and golden bells (Exodus 28:33-34), making it recognizable and impressive during temple service.
2. The word also evokes the extent of the fabric that trails or extends: Isaiah sees the Lord sitting on His throne, and the hems of His robe filled the temple (Isaiah 6:1), an image of His immense glory.
3. By extension, the hem represents majesty, power, and authority. This is why the royal or divine robe impresses with its grandeur.
4. Losing or having the hems of one's robe uncovered symbolizes humiliation and disgrace: in Jeremiah and Lamentations, uncovering the hems signifies revealing someone's nakedness and ignominy (Jeremiah 13:22, 13:26).
H7757.origine: The word shul comes from a Hebrew root that literally means "to swing" or "to sway," hence the idea of a part of clothing that hangs, floats, or trails. The concept is visual and tactile: it is what moves and is seen. The same root appears in words designating the hem, fringe, or what is suspended.
H7757.emploi: The word appears ten times in the Old Testament, mostly concentrated in descriptions of the high priest's garment (Exodus 28 and 39). These occurrences detail the ornamentation of the priestly robe: alternating pomegranates and bells around the entire hem. Isaiah 6:1 uses it to magnify the divine presence: the hems of the Lord's garment fill the temple, suggesting a glory that overflows and fills the entire space. In the prophetic passages of Jeremiah, Lamentations, and Nahum, the word takes on a negative symbolic value: uncovering the hems becomes a sign of shame, judgment, and humiliation (Jeremiah 13:22, 13:26, Lamentations 1:9, Nahum 3:5).
H7757.portee: This word reminds us that, in biblical thought, clothing is not merely a practical utensil: it embodies status, honor, and presence. The hems of the high priest's garment, adorned with symbols of God's service, remind us that one who approaches God must be clothed in dignity and holiness. The image of the hems of God's robe filling the temple invites us to contemplate His majesty that exceeds all measure. Finally, the symbolism of humiliation related to nakedness or the uncovering of the hems teaches us that God sees and judges, but also that shame is never the last word: it calls for repentance and restoration.

sens: without shoes, barefoot
stripped of possessions, deprived of necessities
captive, taken into slavery
troubled, disoriented
H7758.detail:
1. Literally, one who is barefoot, without shoes. This is the most direct meaning, used by Micah when he speaks of walking "barefoot and naked" as a sign of mourning and lamentation (Micah 1:8).
2. One who has been stripped, deprived of what protected or belonged to him—his possessions, dignity, freedom. The image extends figuratively: to be "barefoot" is to be reduced to a state of misery.
3. A prisoner, a captive taken far from home, in chains. God "takes captive the counselors" and "the priests" (Job 12:17 and 12:19)—He strips them of their authority and freedom.
4. One whose mind is confused, troubled, deprived of clarity. Job speaks of judges whose reason God "troubles": they lose their assurance and judgment, like someone who walks barefoot and stumbles.
H7758.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of stripping or depriving. Walking without shoes was in ancient Near Eastern culture a visible sign of poverty, captivity, or deep mourning: one would remove their sandals as a sign of humiliation or great suffering. The word thus evokes the concrete image of the bare foot that exposes vulnerability and dependence.
H7758.emploi: This word appears three times in the Old Testament, always in the prophets or in the wisdom literature. Micah uses it to describe his prophetic act of mourning: he will walk "barefoot and naked" as a living lament for the misfortune of Israel. Job, on the other hand, uses it figuratively to depict how God deprives the great of their power: He "troubles" them, makes them "captive," reduces them to impotence. The word thus oscillates between the concrete meaning (being barefoot) and the figurative meaning (being deprived of one's greatness, stability, freedom).
H7758.portee: This word reminds the reader that true strength and dignity do not come from outward appearance or human power. Walking "barefoot" was a shame; but for Micah, it is the prophetic price of solidarity with the suffering. For Job, it shows that God alone controls destinies and can bring the power of the great to nothing. It is an invitation to seek stability not in honors or riches, but in trust in God.

sens: Beloved woman of the Song of Songs
H7759.detail: The Shulammite is the heroine of the Song of Songs, the young woman whose beloved celebrates her beauty and love in this poetic book of the Bible. When the king addresses her in Song of Songs 7:1, he calls her by this name and invites his friends to behold her in a dance.
H7759.origine: The name Shulammite likely means "the peaceful one" or "the perfect one." It appears linked to the place or people of Shulem, although its exact origin remains debated among scholars. What matters for the reader is that it designates a woman from Galilee or the North, probably a shepherdess or a young girl of modest means.
H7759.emploi: The name appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Songs 7:1, where the beloved tenderly calls her and presents her before the spectators. It is one of the passages where the beloved emotionally celebrates each part of the body of the one he loves, in a poetic tableau of mutual desire and admiration. The Song of Songs features this woman as an equal to the king, free to express her love.
H7759.portee: The Shulammite represents for the believer the image of one who is loved by God and who can also love freely. In Christian tradition, she has often symbolized the Church or the faithful soul in union with Christ. The Song of Songs shows that human love, when pure and mutual, is honored in God's creation.

sens: Physically placing something or someone in a location
Directing towards a goal, orienting
Instituting, establishing, founding, constituting
Transforming into, rendering
Imposing or inflicting
Legally constituting in charge, in function
H7760A.detail:
1. Placing or putting: this is the concrete act of setting an object or person somewhere. "You shall make a window for the ark" (Genesis 6:16) means to construct and place that opening. "Place it on a pole" (Numbers 21:8): the bronze serpent is physically placed on a pole for the Israelites to look at.
2. Directing, orienting towards: turning something in the direction of a goal or person. "Set your face toward the mountains of Israel" (Ezekiel 6:2) means to orient one's attention and prophetic word towards that place.
3. Establishing, instituting or founding: creating something that lasts, a structure, a covenant, a law, a function. "You shall establish streets for yourself in Damascus" (1 Kings 20:34): creating and organizing commercial spaces. "I will make his offspring eternal" (Psalms 89:30): establishing a lineage forever.
4. Transforming or rendering: changing the nature or status of something. "I will make you an ornament forever" (Isaiah 60:15): transforming a once-desolate city into beauty and pride.
5. Imposing or applying: putting in place a penalty, an obligation, or an effect. "The Lord placed a mark on Cain" (implied) is a use of the verb to inflict or mark.
6. Appointing to a position: establishing someone in a function. "Samuel appointed his sons as judges" (1 Samuel 8:1): constituting them in an official role.
H7760A.origine: The verb שׂוּם (sum) comes from a very ancient Semitic root meaning "to place, to put." It expresses the fundamental action of putting something in place. The verb can be conjugated in various ways (Qal simple, Hiphil causative, Hophal passive), allowing it to cover a wide range of actions: from physical placement to the creation of abstract structures (laws, covenants, functions). This root is found in other Semitic languages and illustrates how a concrete verb enriches itself by taking on a figurative meaning of "constituting, establishing."
H7760A.emploi: The verb שׂוּם is one of the most frequent in the Old Testament (265 occurrences). It appears everywhere: in Genesis when God establishes the order of the world, in Exodus during the arrangement of the Tabernacle, in the historical books for appointments or covenants, in the Psalms and the prophets to express God's action of creating, transforming, or directing. Its meaning varies according to the context: "make a window" (Genesis 6:16) is technical placement; "establish streets" (1 Kings 20:34) pertains to institution; "make you an ornament" (Isaiah 60:15) expresses transformation. The verb thus unites the concrete and the abstract, human and divine action, and appears as often regarding men as it does regarding God.
H7760A.portee: This verb reveals the power of action: each "to do" or "to place" is an act of creation, organization, or transformation. For the Christian reader, it shows how God not only creates but orders, institutes, and transforms according to His purpose. Even in ordinary human actions, placing, establishing, directing are gestures that participate in the order desired by God. The verb invites us to see each responsible act — placing a stone, establishing justice, transforming a situation — as participation in the divine work of bringing order to the world.

sens: Sign or manifestation of malice
Facial expression that denotes anger or discontent
H7760B.detail:
1. The word designates a visible sign of misfortune or calamity — something that betrays a malicious intent or adverse fate. It is a mark, a trace that is seen and inspires fear. In 2 Samuel 13:32, Jonadab tells the king that only Amnon is dead, which contradicts the bad news brought by the messengers: one must read the "mark of malice" on the faces of the messengers to understand that they bring an exaggerated report.
2. More specifically, it is a facial expression — a grimace or a frown — that betrays anger, disagreement, or a hostile disposition. It is what is read on a person's face when something displeases them or when they wish harm upon someone.
H7760B.origine: The word comes from the root שׂום (siym), which means "to place, to put, to fix." A "sign placed" becomes a visible "mark," particularly a facial expression that cannot be hidden. Words from the same family denote the action of fixing, establishing, or placing something durably. The concept evokes the idea that a bad feeling or malice is "inscribed" on the face and cannot remain hidden.
H7760B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Samuel 13:32, in the dramatic context of the story concerning Amnon and Tamar. Jonadab, a wise man, interprets the troubled silence and expression of the king's messengers: he reads on their features a "mark of malice" that prompts him to comfort David by telling him that only Amnon is dead, not all the king's sons as the messengers seem to imply. The word captures that moment when a violent emotion (anger, bad intent) is involuntarily betrayed by the body.
H7760B.portee: This word reminds us that our emotions and intentions are read on our faces: it is difficult to hide anger, hostility, or malice for long. For the believer, this speaks to the importance of sincerity and guarding the heart, for "out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks" — and also the face. It is an invitation to examine our thoughts and feelings before they betray us.

sens: Place, set something in a location or on someone
Install someone in a position, a role
Express a word or a will in someone
Cause, perform, accomplish an action or a change
Fix, establish a rule, a covenant, or a boundary
Orient, direct towards a goal or a person
H7760H.detail:
1. To place or set an object physically in a location: "The Lord God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and there he put the man whom he had formed" (Genesis 2:8). The verb evokes the concrete gesture of depositing, installing.

2. To name, establish someone in a responsibility or power: "Choose from among all the people capable men... and set them over them as chiefs of thousands, chiefs of hundreds" (Exodus 18:21). It constitutes someone in authority.

3. To put a word, a thought in the heart or mouth of someone, as if God were depositing his message there: "The Lord met Balaam; he put words in his mouth" (Numbers 23:16).

4. To accomplish, realize, perform an action or produce an effect: "They performed wonders in their midst by his power" (Psalms 105:27). The verb describes the action of making something come to pass.

5. To fix, establish definitively a rule, an order, or a command that lasts: when God "puts" his words, he makes them stable and binding.

6. To orient or direct towards: to place something in a direction or in relation to a person, such as "putting one's eyes on" someone or "putting one's trust" in someone.
H7760H.origine: The Hebrew verb sum comes from an ancient root meaning "to place, to set." It is very common throughout the Hebrew Bible. The verb primarily expresses the physical and concrete action of depositing an object, but it then extends to figurative uses: establishing someone in charge, fixing a rule, accomplishing a purpose. This richness of meaning reflects the fluidity of Hebrew, which does not sharply oppose the concrete and the abstract.
H7760H.emploi: Sum appears 229 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is used in almost all the books, particularly in Genesis, Exodus, and Kings. In Genesis, it describes the concrete action of placing or setting objects and people. In Exodus and Leviticus, it often refers to the setting up of the tabernacle and sacred objects. In the historical books (Samuel, Kings), it expresses the establishment of people in charge (judges, leaders, priests). The verb gradually broadens its scope: it means not only to place physically but also to constitute, establish, fix a divine order. In the prophets, it takes on a powerful meaning: God "puts" his word in the mouth of the prophet or "puts" his judgments into action. In all contexts, the verb suggests an action of power and will.
H7760H.portee: This verb invites the reader to understand that God leaves nothing to chance: he places, establishes, orders. When the Bible says that God "puts" something or someone, it affirms his sovereign authority and his positive action in history and in hearts. For the believer, this means that his position, mission, words, and thoughts can be ordered by God; it is a source of confidence and responsibility.

sens: place, set or install physically
take, grasp
expose to danger, risk
demand, require
prepare, get ready to act
establish, fix, constitute or designate
H7760I.detail:
1. To place, set or install physically: the most concrete meaning of the verb, like putting something in a specific location. Jael "took the hammer in hand" (Judges 4:21): she grasped the tool to hold it.
2. To take, grasp: to seize something in hand, often with an intention to act. The king's servants "will lay hands on all that you have of value" (1 Kings 20:6), meaning they will seize your goods.
3. To expose to danger, risk: to put forward, risk one's life or person. Jephthah says, "I have exposed my life" (Judges 12:3): he has put himself in direct peril.
4. To demand, require: to impose a burden or obligation on someone. "You shall not demand interest from him" (Exodus 22:25): do not impose an additional debt on him.
5. To prepare, get ready to act: to put oneself in a state to do something. Ben-Hadad tells his servants, "Make your preparations" (1 Kings 20:12): get yourselves ready for battle.
6. To establish, fix, constitute or designate: to give something its status, order, or function. This is where the verb creates a new reality or assigns a mission.
H7760I.origine: The Hebrew verb שׂוּם (sum) comes from a root that expresses the idea of an action that is placed, resolved, and ordered. It shares this family with other words related to setting up and establishing. In Greek, this verb can be translated as τίθημι (titthèmi), "to place, to set," which carries the same range of meanings: from the physical gesture to the act of instituting. The Hebrew root always emphasizes the idea that one "places" something or someone with intention, fixing it in a state or position.
H7760I.emploi: The verb שׂוּם appears 8 times in these provided usages, mostly in the historical books (Judges, Samuel, Kings) and in the Law (Exodus). Each usage reveals a nuance: in Exodus 22:25, it is the demand for a burden (not to demand interest); in Judges 4:21, it is the act of seizing a weapon; in Judges 12:3 and 1 Samuel 19:5, it is risking one's life in battle; in 1 Kings 20:6, it is putting hands on something to take it; in 1 Kings 20:12, it is preparing, getting ready. The verb thus adapts to the context: it can mean a simple act of placing, a voluntary and courageous act (risking), a demand, or a threatening action. This flexibility reflects the central role of the verb in biblical Hebrew: it is a very frequent verb that serves a thousand uses.
H7760I.portee: This verb invites the reader to meditate on responsibility and intention: when one "puts" or "places" something, one acts. In passages where it involves "risking one's life" (Judges 12:3, 1 Samuel 19:5), this word honors courage and commitment to God and his people. When it designates the demand for interest (Exodus 22:25), it calls for justice towards the poor. This basic, discreet but omnipresent verb reminds us that every action taken has weight: nothing is put in place without consequence.

sens: To put, place, set something or someone in a location or position
To direct, orient towards a direction or goal
To establish, found, institute, constitute
To attribute to someone a fault, a crime, a word that they contest
H7760J.detail:
1. Originally, the verb means the physical act of putting something in a place: to lay a stone, to place a person. It is the concrete action of giving a position or destination to an object or person (Deuteronomy 22:14, where the husband "puts" an accusation against his wife).
2. The verb can also mean to direct or orient towards: to turn one's heart, one's gaze, or even one's compassion in a certain direction. It conveys the idea of intentionally directing something towards a goal.
3. In a legal or institutional context, suma means to institute, found, establish a law or a charge. One "puts" something as a foundation or as a lasting rule.
4. When something is imputed to someone, one "puts" or "attributes" a fault, a word, an action that they deny or contest. In Job 24:25, "who will deny me" literally means "who will nullify what I put" — who will contest or refute the words that I have established as true.
H7760J.origine: The root שׂוּם (sum) fundamentally expresses the action of placing, putting, fixing. It appears in other forms where it always conveys this idea of positioning or constitution: one "puts" foundations, one "puts" an accusation, one "puts" a law. In the Greek Septuagint, this verb is often rendered by τίθημι (tithèmi), which has exactly the same concrete and figurative meaning: to put, place, constitute, establish.
H7760J.emploi: In biblical Hebrew, שׂוּם is extremely frequent and covers a wide range of uses. The context here isolates three uses from the legal or judicial domain: imputing a fault to someone. In Deuteronomy 22:14 and 22:17, it concerns a husband who "imputes" criminal things to his wife, meaning he "puts" or "attributes" the accusation of not being a virgin — a serious accusation that she contests. In Job 24:25, the verb appears in the sense of "putting a word as true": Job challenges who could "deny" him, nullify what he "puts" as a statement. In these three cases, the accusation or affirmation is something that one "establishes" against someone or that one "puts" as fact.
H7760J.portee: This verb teaches the importance of not lightly attributing to others faults or words that dishonor them, as it is to "put" a serious burden on them. In justice, to impute is to accuse, and the accusation must be true and just. For the believer, this reminds us of the responsibility of our words and the call not to bear false witness, not to "put" on others what is not established as true.

sens: To put, place, set something somewhere
To direct one's attention towards, to pay attention to, to take heed
To estimate, judge, take into account, evaluate
To establish, fix, determine, institute
To transform into, to make become, to constitute
H7760K.detail:
1. In the concrete and primary sense: to physically place, to put an object or person in a location — for example, to lay hands on someone (1 Samuel 21:12: David "took" this matter to heart, meaning he placed it within him, engraved it in his mind).

2. To turn one's attention towards something, meaning to notice, observe, pay attention. The Lord "noticed" Job (Job 1:8): He looked upon him, observed him with attention. This is also the sense referred to in Isaiah 42:25: Israel "did not take heed" to the anger of God — they did not pay attention, did not notice.

3. To consider in the sense of judging, estimating, forming an opinion. Nabal "does not take heed" (1 Samuel 25:25): he despises, he does not take into account the one who stands before him. It is to examine internally and form a judgment.

4. To establish, fix, set in place definitively — particularly laws, ordinances, rules. God "considers" His sanctuary (Ezekiel 44:5): the Lord asks Ezekiel to be attentive and to observe well, to direct his mind towards that place.

5. To transform, to make become, to constitute into something new — this is the creative or transformative action of the verb, which also ranks this usage among the "acts of will" that establish a new state.
H7760K.origine: The Hebrew verb שׂוּם (sum) comes from a primary root that expresses the action of putting, placing. Its basic image is very concrete: to arrange something in space. From this root, the meaning first extends to the action of "putting in place" in a figurative sense (establishing a law, constituting a king), and then to that of "putting one's attention" (that is, directing one's mind towards), which explains the meanings of "noticing" and "considering." Words from the same family include the noun שׂוּם (sum, "estimation, judgment"). In classical Hebrew, this verb is one of the most productive and common for expressing the action of constituting, establishing, or directing.
H7760K.emploi: The verb שׂוּם appears 25 times in the provided biblical uses, mostly in the Prophets and the Writings (Job, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Haggai, Malachi) and also in the historical Old Testament (Deuteronomy, Samuel, Kings). Its usage unfolds along an arc: first the concrete sense of "taking, placing, holding" (Deuteronomy 32:46: "Take to heart"), then towards the attentional sense of "noticing, observing" (Job 1:8: God "noticed" Job; Job 34:23: God does not need to "observe for long"), and finally towards the decisive action of "establishing, instituting" (Haggai). The context determines each time the nuance: before God, it is often the divine action of seeing and judging; before men, it is paying attention or evaluating. The translation thus varies between "to take," "to consider," "to notice," "to observe," reflecting the richness of a verb that encompasses both physical action and mental action.
H7760K.portee: This word invites the reader to understand that paying attention is an act of will that can transform. When God "notices" Job, it is never passive: it is a gaze that counts, weighs, judges. For the believer, "considering" calls for the moral effort to observe the Word of God (Deuteronomy 32:46: "Take to heart"), not to remain indifferent. And conversely, there is grace in knowing that the Lord "notices" us, "considers" us: our life does not escape His attention. This verb unites visible action (placing, putting) and hidden action (judging, estimating), reminding us that God sees to the heart.

sens: Physically place something or someone in a specific location
Appoint a person to a position, entrust them with a responsibility or command
Institute, found, create something in a stable and lasting manner
Orient, direct towards a goal or direction
H7760L.detail:
1. Physically place: the word describes the action of putting or placing something somewhere — for example, laying hands on someone, or installing people in a job position. In Exodus 1:11, Pharaoh "established" taskmasters over the Hebrews, meaning he placed them in charge to oversee them.
2. Entrust a function: install someone in a role, an official responsibility. In 1 Samuel 10:19, the people ask Samuel: "Establish a king over us!", meaning designate someone who will be king. In 2 Samuel 17:25, Absalom "appointed" Amasa as the head of the army.
3. Institute or found: create something established, permanent, and stable. This is to establish rules, laws, an order that lasts — as one "establishes" a king forever on the throne of Israel (2 Samuel 7:10).
4. Orient or direct: turn something towards a direction, a goal. Proverbs 8:29 speaks of the one who "establishes" a boundary for the sea, meaning he sets its contours and borders.
H7760L.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that evokes the idea of placing, putting, setting firmly. The word belongs to the family of concrete action verbs — it has no distant etymology but expresses a fundamental notion in daily and administrative life: putting someone or something in its place. In the Greek of the Old Testament (Septuagint), it is often translated by verbs like "tithémi" (to place, to establish), showing that all biblical languages share this image of placement and institution.
H7760L.emploi: This verb appears 24 times in the provided texts, mainly in historical and legislative books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Exodus, Deuteronomy). In the political context, it refers to the establishment of a king, a leader, or an officer (1 Samuel 8:5, 10:19; Deuteronomy 17:15). In the administrative context, it describes the installation of foremen or work leaders (Exodus 1:11, 5:14). In the liturgical context, it can mean the establishment of lasting rules or practices (Psalms 78:5). The meaning varies slightly depending on whether one speaks of placing people, material things, or institutions: physically placed, put into function, or instituted in a stable manner.
H7760L.portee: This word shows how God and men "establish" social and political order. It reminds us that authorities, laws, and structures do not arise from nothing: someone puts them in place. For the reader, this raises the question of obedience to those who have been established, but also the responsibility of the one who establishes: entrusting power means being accountable before God.

sens: Place, put, set something in position
Establish, fix, constitute someone or something permanently
Assign, confer a name to someone or something
Present, expose, communicate a meaning or interpretation
H7760M.detail:
1. The basic concrete meaning: to place or put something in a specific location, to set it in position. This is the material action of giving a place to an object ("they read distinctly from the book of the law of God, and they gave the sense of it," Nehemiah 8:8).
2. Establish or constitute someone in a function, a condition, a lasting dignity — making someone something important and permanent. Jacob becomes Israel not by chance, but because God "gave him the name of Abraham" (Nehemiah 9:7), which means assigning him a new and definitive identity.
3. Assign, impose a name on someone or something. The chief of the eunuchs "gave names" to the Hebrew captives, replacing their identities with new ones (Daniel 1:7). This is an act of power: to name is to master and redefine.
4. Present or expose a meaning, an explanation, an interpretation. The Levites "gave the sense" of the text of the law so that the people could understand (Nehemiah 8:8) — they placed the text under the light of a clear explanation.
H7760M.origine: The Hebrew verb שׂוּם (sum) comes from a very ancient root related to the idea of placing, putting in position. Its basic image is physical and material: taking something and putting it somewhere. From this derive all the figurative meanings: establishing a law, constituting someone in a role, or assigning a name — all acts of definitive placement. The root encompasses the idea that to give is to set in place intentionally and often durably.
H7760M.emploi: This verb is very frequent in biblical Hebrew. In the four provided occurrences, the dominant meaning is that of "giving a name" or "assigning an identity": God calls Jacob by the name of Israel (2 Kings 17:34; Nehemiah 9:7), and the chief of the eunuchs gives Babylonian names to the young Hebrews (Daniel 1:7). One occurrence broadens the meaning: "giving the sense" means exposing, interpreting, making understood (Nehemiah 8:8). The context always shows an act of authority or power: the one who "gives" a name or an explanation exercises a form of control or leadership. The verb is also used for material acts (putting in place) and spiritual or institutional acts (establishing, constituting).
H7760M.portee: This word reveals to the reader the power of language and name in biblical thought. Naming someone is not simply labeling: it is redefining their identity and destiny. When God "gives" a name, it is a creative and transformative act. Similarly, "giving the sense" invites believers to see that understanding Scripture does not happen in isolation, but through interpretation received and transmitted communally. For the Christian, this reminds us that our identities, our spiritual names, are divine gifts that redefine us.

sens: Issue an official command, a directive
Grant authorization, permission
Establish, set a decree or rule
Decree, order something by authority
H7761G.detail:
1. Issue an official command: this is the sense of one who has power and makes known their will. King Cyrus "gives" the order to rebuild the temple (Ezra 5:13); King Darius "gives" the order to search the archives (Ezra 6:1). This is the act of one who commands.
2. Grant authorization: the word is used when permission is requested to do something. The governors ask: "Who gave you the authorization to build this house?" (Ezra 5:3), meaning: who gave you the official permission?
3. Establish or set a decree: the king issues an edict, a rule that imposes itself. Darius "gives" the order regarding what the officials will do for the construction of the temple (Ezra 6:8), setting the rules and means.
4. Decree, order by sovereign authority: the supreme authority lays down its decision as law. Darius says, "I, Darius, have given this order. Let it be executed punctually!" (Ezra 6:12), affirming his absolute power over what must be done.
H7761G.origine: This Aramaic verb comes from a simple root meaning "to place" or "to put." The word implies an action by one who has authority: one only "gives order" if they have the right to command. In the Aramaic Bible, it is used almost exclusively for the orders of Persian kings, showing its close link with the exercise of political and administrative power.
H7761G.emploi: The verb appears eighteen times in the Aramaic New Testament, almost exclusively in Ezra and Daniel. It designates each time an act of authority: the Persian kings (Cyrus, Darius) who give orders to rebuild the temple, who authorize or prohibit, who punish or reward. In Ezra 4:19; 5:13; 6:1, it is the order for a search or construction. In Ezra 5:3, it is the question of the authorization granted. In Daniel 3:10; 6:26, the royal order takes on the force of law that must not be transgressed. The word is never used for an ordinary act: it always reserves the idea of power exercised officially.
H7761G.portee: This word reminds us that true authority comes from above, from a legitimate power. For the biblical reader, seeing the Persian kings "give order" to rebuild the temple shows that even the powerful of the world often accomplish, often unknowingly, what God has planned. It is a lesson in trust: human obstacles to God's work are never definitive.

sens: Man of the tribe of Asher, before the monarchy of Israel
H7763H.detail: 1. Schomer is a man of the tribe of Asher mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:32. He is the son of Heber and the brother of Japhlet, Hotham, and Shua. His name literally means "guardian" in Hebrew, but it refers here to a man in the genealogy of Asher.
H7763H.origine: The name Schomer comes from the Hebrew root שמר (shamar), which means "to keep," "to observe," "to protect." This root is very common in the Bible and gives rise to words like "guard," "guardian," "observance." The name Schomer was borne by several men in ancient Israel; it often expresses a function of protection or vigilance. The variant Shémer (שֶׁ֫מֶר) designates the same type of character or an alternative form of the name.
H7763H.emploi: Schomer is mentioned only once in the biblical genealogies, in 1 Chronicles 7:32, as the son of Heber in the lineage of Asher. He appears within a genealogical list that enumerates the families of the tribe of Asher before the establishment of the Israelite monarchy. The Bible places him in an ancient time, prior to the reign of Saul. Although nothing else is known about his life or deeds, he is thus inserted into the genealogical memory of Israel.

sens: son of Gad and ancestor of a tribe of Israel
founder of the family of the Schunites
H7764.detail:
1. Schuni is one of the seven sons of Gad, one of the twelve sons of Jacob. His name appears in the list of Jacob's descendants who came to Egypt with him (Genesis 46:16), where he is listed among his brothers Ziphion, Haggi, Etsbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli.
2. Schuni became the founder and eponymous ancestor of the family of the Schunites, one of the families descended from the tribe of Gad. This lineage is confirmed at the time of the census of the people of Israel in the wilderness, where the descendants of Schuni are listed as a distinct family within Gad (Numbers 26:15).
H7764.origine: The name Schuni means "fortunate" or "happy" in Hebrew. It is a personal name that marks the identity of a man and his descendants. His brother Arodi and his other brothers also receive Hebrew names that characterize important individuals in the genealogy of Israel.
H7764.emploi: Schuni is mentioned twice in the Bible, both in important genealogical contexts. The first mention is found in Genesis 46:16, where he appears in the list of Gad's children who accompany Jacob to Egypt during the great famine. The second mention is in Numbers 26:15, during the census of the new generation in the wilderness, where his descendants form the family of the Schunites, one of the four main families of Gad at that time in Israel's history.

sens: Descendants of Schuni, son of Gad
H7765.detail: The Schunites are the members of the family clan descended from Schuni, son of Gad. Schuni was one of the sons of Gad listed during the descent into Egypt (Genesis 46:16), and at the time of the census in the wilderness, his descendants formed a family among the tribes of Israel (Numbers 26:15). Like the other family groups descended from the sons of Gad, the Schunites are counted among the people of God organized into family clans.
H7765.origine: Schuni means "fortunate" or "happy" in Hebrew. The Schunites bear the name of their ancestor Schuni, the first son of Gad mentioned in the genealogy. The Hebrew suffix -i indicates belonging to a family or tribal group. Similarly, each son of Gad gave rise to a family (Tsephonites, Haggites, Ebonites, Ezrites, Erodites, Arelites), together forming the twelve families of the tribe of Gad.
H7765.emploi: The Schunites appear only once in the Bible, at the time of the census of the people of Israel in the wilderness, after the exodus from Egypt. They are listed among the families of the tribe of Gad, one of the twelve tribes. This census shows how the people of Israel, descended from the twelve sons of Jacob, multiplied into distinct family clans despite the generations.

sens: City of Issachar in Israel, located south of Mount Tabor
H7766.detail: Sunem is a city that belongs to the tribe of Issachar, in the northern part of the land of Israel (Joshua 19:18). It is located about 8 kilometers south of Mount Tabor. It is a place of passage for prophets: Elisha regularly comes there to eat with a wealthy woman from the city (2 Kings 4:8). It is also a strategic location: the Philistines set up their camp there before the battle of Gilboa where Saul meets his death (1 Samuel 28:4).
H7766.origine: The name Sunem literally means "double resting place" in Hebrew. It designates a well-established city, a known stopping point in the journeys of travelers and prophets.
H7766.emploi: Sunem appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first listed among the cities of the tribe of Issachar (Joshua 19:18). It becomes famous as the place where the Philistines set up their military camp before their confrontation with Saul and the Israelites (1 Samuel 28:4). In the prophetic context, it is known as the home of a generous woman who welcomes the prophet Elisha whenever he passes through the city (2 Kings 4:8).

sens: Inhabitant of Sunem, city of Galilee
H7767.detail: Term designating a woman from Sunem, a city in northern Israel. The word simply indicates geographical origin or belonging to this locality, just as one would say "a Galilean" or "a Judean." Biblical references mention two famous Sunamites: Abishag, who served King David in his old age (1 Kings 1:3), and the woman of the learned man whom the prophet Elisha visited (2 Kings 4:12).
H7767.origine: The word comes from Sunem (שׁוּנֵם), whose meaning is probably "double resting place" (double abode or double resting place in Hebrew). The feminine suffix -ית (-it) indicates a woman from this place, according to the common pattern in Hebrew. Sunem was a city in the territory of the tribe of Issachar, in northern Galilee.
H7767.emploi: The term appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in the narratives of the books of Kings. Abishag the Sunamite (1 Kings 1:3, 1:15, 2:17, 2:21, 2:22) is presented as a beautiful young girl chosen to care for the aged King David. After his death, one of his sons attempts to obtain Abishag, which provokes Solomon's anger (2 Kings 2:17-22). Another Sunamite appears in 2 Kings 4, a prosperous woman who welcomed Elisha and was blessed with the birth of a son.
H7767.portee: These narratives remind us that biblical characters have concrete origins and that genealogy matters in the biblical world. The figure of Abishag also shows how the Bible honors respect for the elderly (David receives care from a young woman), while the Sunamite of Elisha embodies generous hospitality and faith that attracts divine blessings.

sens: Call for help with a loud and urgent voice
Implore, beg someone (especially God) with urgency
Demand justice or assistance by crying out
Let out a cry, an intense vocal sound
File a complaint or express grievances loudly
H7768.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to cry out loudly, to raise one's voice forcefully to be heard from afar or to express intense emotion. It is the physical act of making noise with one's voice, often in urgency: Job 30:20 says, "I cry out to you," expressing the desperate call of the supplicant.

2. The word takes on a more religious meaning when it refers to the act of imploring God or someone else. It is calling for help with intensity and insistence, counting on someone to listen. Psalms 30:3 says, "I cried to you, and you healed me": it is an act of supplication directed towards God.

3. Crying out for justice or help: demanding loudly that a wrong be righted or that assistance be given. Job 19:7 shows this: "I cry out against violence, but no one answers" — it is crying out that one is a victim of injustice.

4. The word can simply refer to a vocal noise, a cry made by a creature (Job 39:3 speaks of the cry of wild beasts).

5. Filing a complaint, expressing distress by crying out: Habakkuk 1:2 says, "I cry out to you, but you do not listen" — it is complaining forcefully about one's situation.
H7768.origine: The Hebrew verb שׁוַע comes from a root that evokes the idea of raising one's voice, of crying out loudly. The form used here is the Piel (intensive form), which reinforces the idea: it is not just a simple noise, but a strong, repeated, insistent cry. The word has a nuance of supplication, of urgent calling, often directed to God or to demand justice. It is a cry that seeks a response, that waits to be heard.
H7768.emploi: The verb appears 21 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Psalms and the book of Job, where it describes the cries of the unfortunate, the oppressed, and the righteous who implore God. In the Psalms, it is almost always God that one cries out to: the psalmist raises his voice to be heard, hoping for a response and assistance (Psalms 30:3, Psalms 88:14). In Job, the word often expresses the distress of one who cries but remains unanswered (Job 30:20, Job 36:13): it is a cry of urgency that measures the absence of response. Isaiah 58:9 and Jonah 2:3 show that God hears this cry and responds to it. The word recurs in laments and complaints, each time one supplicates with the intensity of pressing need.
H7768.portee: This word reminds us that prayer is not a tranquil word, but sometimes an urgent cry, a supplication made with all its emotion. It validates the moments when faith seeks God insistently, when one is unhappy, oppressed, or destitute. God hears the one who cries out to Him, even when the response is delayed: this verb teaches us that our urgency, our pain, our call for help matters to God.

sens: call for help uttered in misfortune
imploration, urgent request
assistance, relief expected
H7769.detail:
1. The cry of distress is the cry uttered by someone who suffers or is about to perish, a vocal expression of suffering. In Job 30:24, the unfortunate man "does he not implore for help?": the cry itself is the call addressed to God or others.
2. It is also the imploration, the urgent and insistent request. In Job 36:19, the "cries" of a person in anguish could be enough to "bring him out" of his pain: the cry becomes a request for relief.
3. By extension, the word designates the help itself, the aid or salvation that one hopes to receive by crying out. The cry and what one cries for become intertwined: one says "cry" to mean "what one asks for by crying out."
H7769.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of crying out, of letting out a cry. It is related to other Hebrew words meaning "to cry" or "to call." The basic sense is very concrete: it is the noise one makes when calling for help, hence the idea of an urgent request addressed to someone stronger.
H7769.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Job. In Job 30:24, it refers to the imploration of the unfortunate who stretches out his hands for help. In Job 36:19, it refers to the cries uttered by someone in anguish. In both cases, it is the expression of suffering and supplication, in contexts of great distress. The word always evokes the desperate situation of one who has no other recourse but to cry out.
H7769.portee: This word reminds us that the prayer of the believer, especially in suffering, is an authentic cry addressed to God. It is not a polite formula, but the true expression of need and dependence. The text of Job shows that God hears the cry of the suffering one and that this prayer is a form of trust, even in the midst of misfortune.

sens: Canaanite, father of Judah's wife
H7770.detail: Shua is a Canaanite mentioned during the time of the Patriarchs. He is best known as the father of the woman who became Judah's wife: it is in Genesis 38:2 that we encounter him, when Judah "saw the daughter of a Canaanite, named Shua; he took her as a wife." This woman bore him three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah (1 Chronicles 2:3). After his death, mentioned in Genesis 38:12, his direct role disappears from the narrative, but his descendants remain important in the history of Judah and his tribe.
H7770.origine: The name Shua means "wealth" in Hebrew. It designates a Canaanite man living in the time of the Patriarchs, likely a man of good standing or notable status in his region, since he manages to ally with Judah through the marriage of his daughter.
H7770.emploi: Shua appears three times in the Bible: twice in Genesis 38 (verses 2 and 12) and once in 1 Chronicles 2:3. In the account of Genesis 38, he is the father of Judah's Canaanite wife, and his appearance frames the story of the relationship between Judah and Tamar, since the death of his daughter marks a turning point in the narrative. In 1 Chronicles 2, he is recalled as the ancestor of the three sons born from this union. These brief but crucial mentions make Shua an important link in the genealogy of Judah, even though he is never the central character of an action.

sens: Who possesses great wealth, material riches
Who is generous, noble-hearted, magnanimous
H7771A.detail:
1. The word primarily describes one who has wealth, abundant possessions. In Job 34:19, God makes no distinction between the "rich" and the poor in His judgment: He treats all humans equally, without favoring the one who has money.
2. It also means "magnanimous" or "noble," a generosity of heart and soul. In Isaiah 32:5, the prophet announces that in the time of salvation, people who are false or foolish will no longer be given honorable titles like "magnanimous" — true moral qualities will finally be recognized.
H7771A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root expressing abundance and generosity. The primary idea is that of having in abundance, hence material wealth, but also the richness of heart: a rich man can be generous and broad in his feelings. The same root is used to express liberality and nobility of character.
H7771A.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the French translation. In Job 34:19, it refers to the rich in a material sense, in a context of divine justice: God does not favor the rich. In Isaiah 32:5, it takes on the moral nuance of "magnanimous," to designate the nobility of heart that should truly be honored. The word thus oscillates between material wealth and moral richness.
H7771A.portee: This word reminds the reader that true wealth is not primarily that of the purse, but that of the heart. Before God, rich and poor are equal; generosity and magnanimity are the true nobility that should be honored.

sens: A sound produced by the voice to call, warn, or express intense emotion
Alarm cry, call for help
Shout of distress or despair
H7771B.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the sound produced by the human voice — a raw cry, a loud call to be heard from afar. It is a sound emitted with force, in contrast to ordinary speech. In Isaiah 22:5, the "cries" of distress resonate toward the mountain: these are the desperate calls of the inhabitants of Jerusalem in the face of destruction.
2. It is often a cry launched in urgency or danger — a call for help, a warning. This meaning aligns with that of a war cry, shouted to galvanize or alert in a critical moment.
3. The word can also evoke a clamor of suffering, panic, or lamentation — the sound emitted when one is overwhelmed, crushed by events. In its unique biblical usage, this context of distress dominates: the inhabitants cry out in the face of a day of "trouble, crushing, and confusion."
H7771B.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of letting out a sharp cry, of being heard by voice. It belongs to the family of verbs and nouns related to intense vocal noise. The word is rare in the Old Testament, which underscores its expressive force: it designates not ordinary speech, but the spontaneous, raw cry of one who cries out to be heard or to express extreme emotion.
H7771B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 22:5. The prophet describes a terrible day, sent by God, when Jerusalem will be crushed: the walls will be demolished and "cries" of distress will rise toward the mountain. This context of immediate catastrophe, destruction, and collective panic shows that the word here expresses the desperate call of the inhabitants in the face of invasion and the collapse of their city. The rarity of the word in biblical texts suggests that it is reserved for moments of extreme crisis.
H7771B.portee: This word reminds us that in times of great distress, the human voice becomes a cry — a spontaneous expression of panic or supplication. For the biblical reader, it illustrates how God, through His prophets, reveals in advance the consequences of unfaithfulness and judgment. This cry heard by the Lord also calls for repentance and trust in God, even in the midst of misfortune.

sens: nomadic tribe of Mesopotamia
H7772.detail: Shoa designates a nomadic people from Mesopotamia, mentioned in the Bible as one of the nations that the prophet Ezekiel refers to in describing the alliances and threats surrounding the people of Israel. The name appears only once in the Old Testament, in Ezekiel 23:23, where Shoa is cited among other peoples of the ancient Near East.
H7772.origine: The name Shoa means "rich" in Hebrew. It refers to a historical people from Mesopotamia, a group of nomads whose economic and military influence was known in ancient Near Eastern times. The meaning of the name likely reflects their prosperity and commercial or warrior power.
H7772.emploi: Shoa appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 23:23. The prophet mentions it in an oracle where he lists the foreign peoples that threaten Jerusalem or symbolize Israel's religious unfaithfulness. Shoa is listed among other nations of the ancient Near East (Assyrians, Babylonians, Chaldeans, and others), all designated as major military and political powers of that time. This unique mention shows that Shoa was well-known enough to the people of Israel to serve as a reference in prophetic warnings.

sens: vocal call made with force or urgency
sound expression of distress, supplication
urgent request addressed to God
H7773.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the raw cry, the call shouted aloud with urgency or intensity — the very sound produced by one who calls. In Psalms 5:3, the psalmist says to God, "Be attentive to my cries": he imagines that God literally hears his voice rising toward Him.
2. It is often the cry of one who suffers, who is afraid, or who seeks help — a cry of distress or supplication. The context of Psalm 5 shows that it is less about the noise than the emotion that drives it: it is a cry from the heart, a prayer that rises from the depths.
3. In biblical language, this cry becomes a form of prayer, a request addressed to God with insistence. The psalmist does not speak softly: he cries out to his God, raising his voice to be heard and to obtain a response.
H7773.origine: The Hebrew word שׁוַע comes from a root that expresses the idea of crying out, of making calls. This root evokes the physical action of raising one's voice, of calling someone for help. The same word or its close relatives appear in various situations where one cries out — in calling, in distress, in supplication. It is a simple, concrete word that depicts the very gesture of one who cries.
H7773.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible (in Psalms 5:3), but its rarity does not diminish its impact. It describes the cries that the psalmist addresses to God in the morning, in his prayer. The usage shows that biblical prayer is not always silent or restrained: it can be a cry, a passionate and loud expression of request. The psalmist turns to God not by whispering, but by crying out, raising his voice, like one who truly needs to be heard.
H7773.portee: This word reminds the reader that praying is not murmuring timidly, but daring to cry out to God, expressing one's distress or urgency with sincerity. It is an invitation to honesty, to passion in the relationship with God. The Christian's prayer can be a cry, and God promises to hear those who cry out to Him.

sens: spontaneous and intense vocal call
lamentation uttered under pain or distress
supplication addressed to God
sound visibly rising to heaven
H7775.detail:
1. The cry is primarily a powerful vocal call, torn from strong emotion: it is the noise made by the children of Israel groaning under the Egyptian yoke, a cry that bursts forth despite themselves (Exodus 2:23).
2. It is often a lamentation provoked by physical or moral suffering: in Ashdod, the people struck by divine judgment raise cries of distress that reach up to heaven (1 Samuel 5:12).
3. This cry becomes a prayer, a supplication addressed to God: the psalmist cries out to the Lord in his distress, and this cry reaches God's ears as a word heard (2 Samuel 22:7, Psalms 18:7).
4. Finally, the cry is described as rising, reaching God: this image of the cry ascending shows that the distress of the people or the faithful does not remain confined, but reaches heaven and the ears of the Lord who listens (Psalms 34:16, Psalms 39:13).
H7775.origine: The Hebrew word שַׁוְעָה (shavah) comes from a root evoking the intense cry, the call that comes from the depths of one's being. It is a word from the realm of strong emotions and desperate communication. In biblical Hebrew, the cry is often presented as rising to God, an image that expresses that sincere prayer, born of suffering, crosses the distance between heaven and earth.
H7775.emploi: This word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Psalms and in situations of distress. It always designates a spontaneous call, driven by emotion: either the lamentation of the slaves in Egypt (Exodus 2:23), or the cry of the sick or afflicted cities (1 Samuel 5:12), or especially the prayer of the righteous in suffering who confide in God. In all cases, the cry reaches God: His ears are attentive to it (Psalms 34:16), He hears it from His palace (2 Samuel 22:7). The cry here takes on a spiritual dignity: it is not a vain cry, but a word that God receives.
H7775.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that suffering has a voice before God. When words fail, the cry itself is prayer. The Bible assures that God listens not to resigned silence, but to the cry of distress of the righteous. This assurance invites us not to hold back our pain, but to cry it out to the One who hears.

sens: Carnivorous mammal resembling a canine, with reddish fur
Creature that inhabits ruins and devastated places
Pest that destroys crops
Symbol of malice or destructive cunning
H7776.detail:
1. The fox is a wild animal well known to the ancient Israelites, a cunning and carnivorous creature that can also refer to the jackal. Samson catches three hundred of them to use as vengeful weapons (Judges 15:4), or they go to ravage the blooming vineyards (Song of Solomon 2:15).
2. It is a beast of ruins and devastated lands. After the destruction of Jerusalem, foxes roam on the ravaged Mount Zion (Lamentations 5:18), signs of disaster and desolation.
3. The animal destroys vineyards and crops: little foxes ruin the blooming vineyards (Song of Solomon 2:15), and even a single fox can overturn a stone wall (Nehemiah 4:3).
4. Figuratively, the fox represents malice and destruction: false prophets are like foxes among the ruins, digging and undermining (Ezekiel 13:4), an image of their destructive action against the people.
H7776.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of digging or burrowing: the fox is primarily one that digs burrows. In Hebrew, the same word can refer either to the fox in the strict sense or to the jackal, two closely related animals that share this characteristic of prowlers of barren lands and ruins. The Segond translates the word once as "jackal" (Psalms 63:11), highlighting this proximity.
H7776.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the wisdom books and narratives: primarily in the book of Judges where Samson uses them as living weapons, in the Song of Solomon where they symbolize minor damage to the vineyards, in prophetic and lamentation texts where they embody desolation (Lamentations, Ezekiel). Its usage remains consistent: it is always a destructive creature and a sign of misfortune, whether used in the literal sense (the animal itself) or figuratively (the image of destruction or evil). The convergence of these usages shows that the ancient Israelite primarily saw it as a harmful beast, and then, by extension, an image of malice.
H7776.portee: The fox in the Bible reminds us that God notices even the creatures that destroy what He has given, and that desolation does not escape His sight. For the believer, it is an invitation to watch over the small things that ravage their faith or spiritual life, just as foxes ravage blooming vineyards: it is not always the great dangers that cause the most damage, but the small evils that we allow to settle.

sens: Region or territory in ancient Israel
H7777A.detail: 1. Shual designates a territory or region of Israel, mentioned as a geographical landmark during a Philistine military incursion. In 1 Samuel 13:17, three Philistine detachments leave the camp to ravage the land, and one of them heads specifically toward the region of Shual, indicating that it was a known and identifiable place at the time of King Saul.
H7777A.origine: The name Shual comes from Hebrew and means "jackal" — a typical animal of the ancient Near East. The territory likely received this name either due to the presence of this animal or as a metaphor. It may also be related to the clan or tribe of Asher, since 1 Chronicles 7:36 mentions a Shual as a son of Zophah, of Asher, suggesting a connection to this region in northern Israel.
H7777A.emploi: Shual appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Samuel 13:17, in the context of a Philistine raiding expedition during Saul's reign. The context indicates that it was a region well-known enough to be specifically mentioned as the destination of a column of raiders, implying some importance or population density. The precise location is not definitively determined by the biblical texts, but it likely lay within the territory of Asher or nearby, in northwestern Israel.

sens: A man from the tribe of Asher during the divided monarchy
H7777B.detail: 1. Shual is a man from the tribe of Asher, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Tsofach and the father of three children: Arah, Hanniel, and Rizia. This genealogy is recorded to preserve the memory of the families of the tribe of Asher during the period when the kingdom of Israel had divided into two rival kingdoms (1 Chronicles 7:36). The name also appears in the form Ulla in a similar genealogical context in the same passage.
H7777B.origine: The name Shual means "jackal" in Hebrew, like many biblical names that evoke animals. It is a descriptive nickname rather than a pure genealogy, a common usage in the Old Testament where names often characterized the person or their distinctive traits. Although the jackal is a wild and cunning animal in ancient Near Eastern culture, we do not know why this man bore this particular name — perhaps due to a resemblance, a quality, or a circumstance of birth.
H7777B.emploi: Shual is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:36, in a genealogical list of the tribe of Asher. These lists of names, which we find mostly in 1 and 2 Chronicles, served to record the descendants of the patriarchs and to establish the rights of families to land and religious functions. Shual is listed among the sons of Tsofach, alongside brothers like Suach and Harnépher. His historical existence is attested only by this passage.

sens: Person responsible for guarding the entrance of a place, especially a temple or palace
One who watches over and protects a threshold or door
Guardian assigned to a regular and organized service
H7778.detail:
1. The porter is one who physically guards access to an important building: temple, royal palace, or other protected place. It is a concrete and visible role. In 2 Samuel 18:26, the sentinel calls out to the porter to signal that a runner is approaching: the porter is therefore at his post, at the entrance, to welcome or stop the arrivals.
2. Beyond mere presence, the porter watches and controls: he decides who enters and who does not exit. In 1 Chronicles 9:22, the porters of the temple thresholds are "recorded in the genealogies" and "established in their functions," which shows the importance and official nature of their role.
3. In the context of the temple and palace, the porter is part of an organized and enduring structure. In 1 Chronicles 16:38 and 2 Chronicles 23:4, the porters work "in rotation" or in regular teams; they are not isolated men but members of a sacred or royal hierarchy.
H7778.origine: The Hebrew word שֹׁעֵר (shoer) comes from the root שׁעַר (sha'ar), which means "door" or "gate." The porter is therefore literally "one who belongs to the door," that is, one who is in charge of it. This root is found in other biblical words designating the gates of the city or the temple. The starting image is that of the door itself: the guardian is defined by his connection to this passage and threshold.
H7778.emploi: The word porter (שׁוֹעֵר) appears 37 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books and notably in 1 and 2 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. It almost always refers to Levites or temple servants tasked with guarding the sacred entrances. In the earliest texts (2 Samuel, 2 Kings), it can refer to a guard of the royal palace or a servant stationed at an important door. From the time of the return from exile (Ezra, Nehemiah), the porter becomes a clearly defined function at the temple, integrated into a genealogy and a service schedule. The context remains one of guarding, access control, and organized order.
H7778.portee: The porter reminds us that access to God, and to His sanctuary, is regulated and serious: it is not a trivial passage. The role of the porter signifies that the house of God has boundaries, that one cannot enter it casually. For the believer, this evokes the holiness of the temple and the respect due to God. It also shows that divine service requires order, faithfulness, and thoughtful organization: everyone in their place, everyone at their time.

sens: Strike with force, grind, crush
Wound, bruise
Assail, rush upon violently
Cover, envelop
H7779.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is the action of striking and crushing something with force, grinding it under weight or a blow. This is what happens when one crushes the head of the adversary: a violent and crushing blow that destroys (Genesis 3:15).
2. The word can also refer to an injury, a bruise: when one is struck, one is wounded. This is why the heel can be bruised in the same verse (Genesis 3:15).
3. To assail means to rush upon someone violently, like a storm descending upon one who is sailing. Job describes how God assails him "like a storm" (Job 9:17), an image of an irresistible force that suddenly descends.
4. The verb can also mean to cover or envelop: darkness threatens to cover the psalmist, to completely envelop him in obscurity (Psalms 139:11).
H7779.origine: This verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of striking, hitting, falling upon. The basic image is that of a force that descends, crushes, or covers. The different meanings (crush, wound, assail, cover) are all nuances of a violent and sudden action, as if something or someone falls upon its target with power.
H7779.emploi: The verb שׁוּף appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of violence or threat. In Genesis 3:15, it describes the eschatological conflict between the offspring of the woman and that of the serpent: a battle where one crushes the head of the other while being wounded in the heel, a symbolic image of total victory despite a wound. In Job 9:17, the same verb expresses the violence of God's assault on Job, comparable to a storm. In Psalms 139:11, it takes on a more metaphorical meaning: to cover, to envelop. These three uses show a verb that always expresses a violent and sudden action imposed from the outside.
H7779.portee: This word appears in one of the most fundamental promises of the Bible: Genesis 3:15, where God announces that the offspring of the woman will crush the head of the serpent. This messianic promise assures that evil will ultimately be defeated, even if victory comes through a wound. For the Christian reader, this passage evokes Christ's victory over Satan, achieved through His death and resurrection.

sens: General of the army of the Syrian king Hadadezer
H7780.detail: Shophach is the commander of the army (military chief) of the Syrian king Hadadezer. He appears in the accounts of David as the commander of the enemy forces. During the battle against David, he is killed in combat (1 Chronicles 19:18).
H7780.origine: The name means "expansion" in Hebrew. It designates a historical figure mentioned in the annals of David's reign, at a time when the monarchy of Israel was consolidated. This same character is called Shobach in other textual variants.
H7780.emploi: Shophach is mentioned twice in the Bible, only in 1 Chronicles 19:16 and 19:18, during David's military campaign against the Syrians. He is presented there as the chief commander of Hadadezer's army. In the first passage, he leads the Syrian reinforcements that come to support the Ammonites; in the second, he is killed during the decisive battle won by David.

sens: descendants of Shupham, son of Benjamin
H7781.detail: The Shuphamites are members of a Benjaminite family, that is, the descendants of Shupham. Shupham was one of the sons of Benjamin, the founding tribe of the southern kingdom. This name designates the family clan descended from this ancestor, listed alongside other Benjaminite families during the census in Numbers 26:39.
H7781.origine: The name Shuphamites comes from Shupham (also called Muppim in Genesis 46:21), one of the ten sons of Benjamin. The suffix -ites (in Hebrew -îm) designates the descendants or members of a family. Shupham can mean "nakedness" or "exposure" in Hebrew. This is a common way in the Bible to form clan names: the suffix is added to the ancestor's name to designate all his descendants.
H7781.emploi: The Shuphamites are mentioned only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:39. This verse lists the families of Benjamin during the second census conducted after forty years of wandering in the desert. Shupham appears there under two name variants: Muppim in Genesis 46:21 (during the first enumeration at the entrance to Egypt) and Shephupham in 1 Chronicles 8:5. The word Shuphamites designates the family clan recorded alongside other Benjaminite families such as the Huphamites and the Ardites.

sens: Musical instrument made from a ram's horn or a trumpet, producing a powerful sound
Sound signal to call, gather, or alert the troops
Sound of the trumpet as a divine call or manifestation of God's power
Musical instrument used for praise and worship to God
H7782.detail:
1. The trumpet is primarily a physical instrument: a horn, usually that of a ram, which produces a loud and distinctive sound. When Joshua besieges Jericho, the priests blow trumpets around the city (Joshua 6:4-6), this powerful and resounding sound being heard from afar.
2. This instrument mainly serves as a military or political signal. Saul "sounded the trumpet throughout the land" to warn the Hebrews of the Philistine threat (1 Samuel 13:3), and when Jehu becomes king, "a trumpet was sounded" to publicly announce his accession to the throne (2 Kings 9:13). It is a quick and effective means to mobilize the population.
3. The trumpet takes on a religious and solemn dimension when it accompanies moments of God's manifestation. At Sinai, "the sound of the trumpet sounded loudly" when God gives His commandments (Exodus 19:16), and this terrifying noise fills the people with dread in the face of the divine presence.
4. In worship and praise, the trumpet becomes an instrument of joy and adoration. Psalm 150 invites to "praise [God] with the sound of the trumpet," and the Jubilee celebration begins when "the trumpet is sounded" throughout the land (Leviticus 25:9), uniting the community in an act of consecration.
H7782.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that primarily designates the material object: an animal horn, particularly that of a ram. The biblical context shows that the trumpet is made from this natural material, hence the term remains linked to the image of the horn. The trumpet appears from the foundational moments of Israel — Sinai, the conquest of Canaan — and remains a central instrument of worship in the Temple, associated with major festivals and solemn calls.
H7782.emploi: The trumpet appears 63 times in the Bible, mainly in the historical books (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings), the Psalms, and the prophets. It serves three main functions: signaling danger or mobilizing warriors (Judges 7:18-22, where the trumpets confuse the enemy; Jeremiah 4:5, where the trumpet is sounded in the face of invasion), celebrating major royal or religious events (David's coronation in 1 Kings 1:34, solemn festival in 2 Chronicles 15:14), and manifesting God's power or presence (Exodus 19:16-19 at Sinai, Joel 2:1 on the day of the Lord). Its use intensifies in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel) as a symbol of divine calling and judgment.
H7782.portee: The trumpet reminds the reader that God does not communicate in silence, but in a loud and sovereign manner. It also symbolizes the importance of hearing and obeying God's call in critical moments of history. For the believer, it evokes the joy of worship and the certainty that God's promises will reach all peoples, even distant nations.

sens: overflow of wealth or profusion
fulfillment of God's promises through the fertility of the land
divine generosity that fills and enriches
H7783.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes the idea of an overflow, a profusion that fills to excess. In Psalms 65:10, God "gives abundance" to the earth by visiting it and filling it with riches — this is the concrete blessing of a harvest that overflows.
2. Abundance manifests the fulfillment of God's promises: when the granaries overflow with grain (Joel 2:24, Joel 3:13), it is a sign that God keeps His commitments and causes His people to prosper.
3. Beyond material wealth, this word expresses the boundless generosity of the Heavenly Father, who does not give in dribs and drabs but generously fills those who fear Him.
H7783.origine: The Hebrew verb shuq comes from a root that fundamentally means "to flow, to overflow." This is why it evokes less the idea of quiet accumulation than of dynamic overflow, like a river in flood. The root expresses the movement of a liquid that fills and exceeds. In the Old Testament, this word paints the blessing under the image of natural fertility and abundant rain that gives life to the earth.
H7783.emploi: The verb shuq appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in contexts of agricultural or eschatological blessing. In Psalms 65:10, it describes how God fertilizes and enriches the earth by visiting it with His presence. In Joel 2:24 and 3:13, it evokes the spectacular overflow of granaries and vats at the time of the final harvest, a sign of judgment and messianic restoration. In all cases, the word emphasizes the superabundant, even excessive, nature of divine blessing — not merely a simple satisfaction of needs, but a profusion that exceeds all expectations.
H7783.portee: This word reminds the believer that God never gives below His promises, but always beyond. The image of overflowing abundance invites trust in His generous Providence and gratitude towards the One who provides without measure. It also encourages waiting for the final fulfillment of divine promises, when justice and blessing will cover the earth.

sens: public way or passage in a city
place of circulation and commercial or social activity
path one walks on
open space in the city as opposed to houses
H7784.detail:
1. The street is primarily the passage or public way that runs through a city, where people walk. It is the space between houses, as in Song of Solomon 3:2, where the young woman goes out into the streets to seek the one she loves.
2. It is also the place of social life and movement: people cross paths, walk, and spend part of their day there. In Proverbs 7:8, the foolish young man passes in the street near a house, walking toward a trap.
3. By extension, it is the path one travels when going from one place to another, the itinerary of someone moving through the city.
4. The street opposes the private dwelling: in Ecclesiastes 12:6-7, death approaches and the man returns from the street to his eternal home, while the mourners walk through the streets after his death.
H7784.origine: The Hebrew word shuq designates the public way or open passage in a settlement. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of circulating or passing. In Greek, the corresponding word in translations is rhumê (ῥύμη) or probably also plateia (πλατεῖα) for wide places.
H7784.emploi: This word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible (Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Solomon). It always designates the public space of the city, where one circulates freely, as opposed to the house or dwelling. In Proverbs 7:8, it is the place where sin lurks, where the young man meets the woman who will seduce him. In Ecclesiastes 12:6-7, it accompanies the image of death: the living walk through the streets, but the dying leaves this public world and is watched over in his final dwelling. In Song of Solomon 3:2, the street and the square are the paths one treads to seek the one they love. The word remains very concrete, never symbolic.
H7784.portee: The street in Scripture is not just a geographical space: it is the place where temptations and encounters unfold, where life flows under the gaze of all. The Christian learns that public and visible life requires vigilance and wisdom, and that every space in this world, even the most ordinary, is a place where one can seek God or turn away from Him.

sens: Part of the lower limb of the body, between the hip and the knee
The thigh or leg of a sacrificial animal
Part of the body struck by illness or marked by weakness
Symbol of strength or capacity
Strength or power of a person
H7785.detail:
