1. The word primarily designates the lower part of the leg or the thigh in humans. In Deuteronomy 28:35, the Lord strikes the "thighs" with a malignant ulcer, showing that this word applies to this fleshy part of the lower limb that can be afflicted by illness.

2. In sacrifices, it specifically refers to the thigh or shoulder of the offered animal, the portion reserved for the priest. Exodus 29:22 speaks of the "right shoulder" of the consecration ram, and Leviticus 7:33 establishes that the "right shoulder" belongs to the priest who offers the thanksgiving sacrifice: it is an honorable share.

3. The leg or thigh also represents the ability to move and physical strength. Psalms 147:10 states that the Lord does not take pleasure "in the legs of man," meaning in human strength or agility.

4. The word can evoke strength or power in general, symbolized by the limb that carries us and enables us to act.
H7785.origine: The Hebrew word shoq comes from a root that refers to the idea of a limb, a part of the body capable of movement and effort. The starting image is that of the leg or thigh as the seat of strength and motor capacity. It is an ancient word from Semitic, also attested in Aramaic (shaq) with the same meaning. In Greek, the Septuagint often renders it as "omos" (shoulder) when it comes to sacrifices, showing that ancient translators understood this term as designating a specific and honorable part of the animal body.
H7785.emploi: The word appears 19 times, primarily in two contexts. First, in the ritual of sacrifices (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers): the shoulder or right thigh of the animal is the portion that the priest receives as a sacred share, sign of his role in worship. Secondly, it applies to the human body, either to describe a part that can be sick or afflicted (Deuteronomy 28:35; Judges 15:8 where Samson kills a thousand), or to evoke strength or agility (Psalms 147:10; Proverbs 26:7 where the legs of the lame hang weak). The meaning varies according to the context: in sacrifices, it is a concrete and honorable share; in poetry or body description, it is either a vulnerable part or the symbol of strength.
H7785.portee: This word reminds us that serving God requires a specific and honorable share: the right shoulder of the sacrifice symbolizes that we give to God what carries us and enables us to act. It also leads us to meditate on our physical fragility — the legs that carry us can be afflicted by suffering — and on the fact that our human strength, whatever it may be, is not sufficient: true power resides in God alone.

sens: To exercise sovereign authority over a people, a territory
To give orders, to decide unilaterally
To struggle forcefully against an opponent, to assert oneself through confrontation
H7786.detail:
1. The primary meaning is political and royal: "to dominate" means to reign, to exercise power over a people or a region. This is what Abimelech does when he "dominates" for three years over Israel (Judges 9:22), asserting his authority as leader over the nation.

2. The word also refers to the act of giving orders, making decisions that impose on others without consultation. This is the meaning in Hosea 8:4: establishing kings "without my order" means acting without divine authorization, without respecting the sovereignty of God who alone has the right to decide.

3. More broadly, "to dominate" can express a struggle, a confrontation where one imposes oneself by force. Jacob "struggled" with the angel (Hosea 12:5): the word describes the intense trial, the confrontation where each seeks to prevail over the other.
H7786.origine: The Hebrew verb שׂוּר (sur) evokes the idea of rising up, asserting oneself, contending. Its root expresses the movement of a person who rises above others, imposing their will. The word belongs to a family of Hebrew terms describing the exercise of power and confrontation.
H7786.emploi: The verb "to dominate" appears three times in the provided texts, always to describe an assertion of authority or force. In Judges 9:22, it denotes the political reign of Abimelech. In Hosea 8:4, it evokes decision-making autonomy, the ability to impose one's choices. In Hosea 12:5, it extends to the personal and spiritual realm: Jacob's struggle becomes an image of perseverance and confrontation in the face of divine will. The word consistently retains the idea of force and prevalence.
H7786.portee: This word reminds the reader that true power belongs to God alone. When Hosea denounces kings established "without his order," he asserts that any human authority that breaks away from God is illegitimate and doomed to failure. The image of Jacob struggling with the angel shows that even the most intense confrontation with God can lead to blessing, provided one does not give up.

sens: To cut with a saw
To tear apart, to cut brutally
H7787.detail:
1. To saw: to cut something with a saw, the toothed blade tool that divides wood or other materials. This is the technical and direct meaning of the verb.
2. To tear apart: the context of 1 Chronicles 20:3 shows that this verb describes a violent and brutal treatment of captives — David "sawed them in pieces" — expressing an execution or extreme punishment. The word here evokes not only the technical action but also the cruel intent and total destruction.
H7787.origine: The Hebrew verb שׂוּר (sur) literally means "to saw." It likely comes from a root expressing the idea of cutting or dividing. The word is rare in the Bible and appears only once, making its exact meaning difficult to establish with certainty, but the context of 1 Chronicles 20:3 confirms its connection to the action of cutting or tearing apart.
H7787.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 20:3, during the account of David's campaign against the Ammonites. David, after his military victory, "brought out the inhabitants, and he sawed them in pieces." This unique usage shows the verb in a context of extreme violence, not in a simple woodworking action. The meaning remains linked to the action of cutting or tearing apart, but applied here to an act of brutal punishment against captives.
H7787.portee: This troubling passage reveals a dark aspect of ancient wars and punishment practices of biblical times. For the Christian reader, it invites reflection on divine justice, the severity of the consequences of rejecting God, and recognizes that Scripture reports historical facts without idealizing them — including violent acts — while inviting the believer to turn towards the mercy and grace revealed in Christ.

sens: To fix one's eyes on something, to observe attentively
To head towards a place, to approach
To travel, to navigate at sea
H7788.detail:
1. To fix one's eyes on something, to observe attentively: the verb primarily expresses the action of directing one's gaze, of contemplating. In the Song of Solomon 4:8, the lover invites his beloved to "look" from the heights of the mountains — he calls her to lift her eyes towards elevated and majestic places.
2. To head towards a place, to approach: the word shifts from the meaning of "to see" to the meaning of "to go towards." In Isaiah 57:9, the one who goes "near" the king literally goes in his direction, towards his presence.
3. To travel, to navigate at sea: the verb is also used to describe the movement of ships. In Ezekiel 27:25, the ships of Tarshish "navigated" for trade — they traversed the seas in search of riches.
H7788.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the movement of sight and movement. The basic image is that of turning one's eyes or body towards something — from which the idea of orienting oneself, heading towards, and then traveling derives. The family includes words related to observation and travel. The original meaning remains partially uncertain, but revolves around this idea of turning towards.
H7788.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Old Testament, each time with a different nuance. In the Song of Solomon, it is the call to contemplate heights. In Isaiah, it is the approach towards a powerful person. In Ezekiel, it is the maritime journey of merchant ships. The three usages show how the word enriches: from visual observation to terrestrial or maritime movement. The context determines the exact meaning each time.
H7788.portee: This word reminds us that "to look" — whether contemplating the beauty of creation, approaching the Lord, or setting out on a journey — is always an action of the whole being. When one "looks" towards God or towards good, one is also moving towards Him. The verb unites the inner desire (the gaze) and the outer commitment (the walk).

sens: To observe, to look at something or someone
To contemplate, to admire by fixing one's gaze
To spy, to watch secretly in order to surprise
To notice, to become aware of
To sing or publicly recount (rare sense)
H7789.detail:
1. To observe, to look at something or someone: this is the simplest meaning — to direct one's eyes toward something to perceive it. Job asks God: "The eye that sees me will see me no more" (Job 7:8), speaking of the one who sees him now but will lose sight of him.
2. To contemplate, to admire by fixing one's gaze: when one looks with attention and admiration, often from a distance. Balaam says of Judah: "I see him from the top of the rocks, I behold him from the heights of the hills" (Numbers 23:9), as if he were observing a people from afar with wonder.
3. To spy, to watch secretly in order to surprise: to look in secret, with malicious intent. Jeremiah denounces those who "spy like a birdcatcher" (Jeremiah 5:26), meaning they observe to set a trap.
4. To notice, to become aware of: simply to realize that something exists or has happened. Job speaks of the place where someone lived: "The place he lived will no longer see him" (Job 20:9).
5. To sing or publicly recount: a very rare sense in the Bible. Job 33:27 uses it when he says that the sinner "sings before men" while confessing his crime.
H7789.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that fundamentally expresses the action of directing one's gaze. The same family of words designates watchers or observers. In Hebrew, there is only one root for "to look" and "to see": it is the same act — to orient the eyes toward an object to perceive it. The verb appears mainly in the poetic and prophetic books, where the gaze is also an act of understanding and judgment.
H7789.emploi: This verb appears 15 times in the provided Old Testament, concentrated mainly in the book of Job (9 occurrences) and a few passages in the prophets. In Job, it often refers to the gaze of God or the wise person observing the world: Job asks to be looked at, weeps for no longer being seen. In the prophets, particularly Jeremiah and Hosea, it takes on a more active hue: to spy, to watch, to contemplate. Balaam uses it to describe his prophetic vision from the heights. The meaning refines according to the context: gazes full of kindness, threatening or furtive gazes, contemplative gazes of the prophet who sees from above.
H7789.portee: This word reminds us that seeing is never neutral: to look is to judge, to know, to be in relationship. For the biblical reader, it raises the question: who sees us? Does God still look at us? Job expresses the anguish of the believer who feels forgotten, while the prophet teaches that God sees everything, even the wicked in their plots. This invites us to reflect on our own gaze upon the world and the awareness of being seen by God.

sens: To look attentively, to observe with care
To follow with one's eyes, to keep a fixed gaze on something or someone
To take an interest in, to pay attention to
H7790.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to look attentively, to observe what is happening before oneself. It is a voluntary and sustained gaze, not a distracted glance. In Psalm 92:12, the psalmist says that his eye delights to "contemplate" his enemies: he observes with interest the situation of those who harm him, probably to see how God acts toward them.
2. The word can also evoke the idea of monitoring, keeping one's eyes fixed on someone or something — from which the sense of "enemy" may emerge, one who observes, who watches (a watcher, a sentinel). This nuance of vigilance or surveillance is contained in the root.
3. On a spiritual level, to contemplate also means to take an interest in, to pay attention: the psalmist shows a real interest in what happens to his adversaries, trusting that God is just.
H7790.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of looking, of fixing the gaze. It is related to the image of the watcher or one who keeps watch, from which the sense of "enemy" (one who looks, who spies) may derive. The root can also be associated with the concept of surveillance or attentive observation.
H7790.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 92:12. In this context, it describes the action of the psalmist who looks at his enemies with satisfaction, confident that God establishes justice. The parallelism of the verse shows that "to contemplate" one's enemies goes hand in hand with "to hear" one's adversaries: it is a conscious and attentive observation of the situation.
H7790.portee: This verse invites the believer to turn his gaze toward God's justice rather than to fear his enemies. To contemplate those who oppose us, in light of divine faithfulness, reassures us and confirms that God watches over His children and rewards the righteous.

sens: fortification, defensive wall of a city
obstacle, barrier to be crossed
wicked, ungodly (figurative or twisted sense)
H7791A.detail:
1. A wall is primarily a stone or brick structure that surrounds a city or camp to protect it from attacks. It is a major defensive construction, thick and tall. In 2 Samuel 22:30 and Psalms 18:30, the psalmist cries out to God: "With my God I can leap over a wall" — the image is that of a warrior who, strengthened by the Lord, can break through the most formidable enemy defenses.
2. By extension, the word designates any obstacle, any barrier that opposes forward movement. A wall thus becomes a symbol of what resists, what blocks. In this figurative sense, one can cross a wall as one overcomes a difficulty or surmounts a trial.
3. In Job 24:11, the word takes an unexpected turn: "in the enclosures of the wicked" — here "wall" seems to designate the wicked person themselves, or their closed and ungodly domain. This is a rare usage, where the meaning strays from the material construction to become almost synonymous with "one who does evil."
H7791A.origine: The Hebrew word שׁוּר (shur) comes from a root that evokes the idea of closing, enclosing, protecting. The word is related to other Hebrew terms expressing enclosure, limit, fence. In the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament), the Greek teichos is found, which carries exactly the same weight: a solid and permanent fortification. The fundamental image is that of a structure that delineates, that separates the inside from the outside.
H7791A.emploi: This word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first used in the literal sense: a wall that is crossed (2 Samuel 22:30 and Psalms 18:30, two parallel passages). In Genesis 49:22, in Jacob's blessing to Joseph, the branches of the fruitful tree "rise above the wall" — probably a poetic image of surpassing, of fertility overflowing. In Job 24:11, the usage becomes enigmatic: the context describes the misdeeds of the wicked, and the word seems to designate the wicked person themselves or their place of closed power. Through these usages, the wall shifts from concrete architecture to figurative: it becomes what opposes, what blocks, what is an obstacle, and ultimately the one who obstructs — the wicked.
H7791A.portee: For the believer reading these psalms, the promise is strong: with God, even the most imposing walls (the most formidable obstacles, the powers that seem unshakeable) can be crossed. It is a call to trust in the strength of the Lord, which infinitely surpasses the material or spiritual obstacles we face. The transition from "wall" to "wicked" in Job also shows how the Bible associates evil with closure, with voluntary confinement outside of grace.

sens: stone or brick structure that encloses and protects a city
defensive and separating barrier
limit, boundary
H7792.detail:
1. The wall is primarily a physical construction: a solid barrier of stone or brick that surrounds a city to protect and delineate it. In Ezra 4:12-13, the adversaries of the Jews inform the king that the walls of Jerusalem are being rebuilt, which would make it a formidable fortress.
2. By its role of defense, the wall is a barrier: it separates the protected city from its surroundings, controlling access and its integrity prevents enemies from entering. This is why raising the walls (Ezra 4:12, 4:16) means restoring the city's ability to defend itself and maintain its independence.
3. Figuratively, the wall represents a limit or boundary: it marks the separation between two territories or powers. In Ezra 4:16, the integrity of the walls symbolizes Jerusalem's autonomy in the face of the Persian king, which threatens his authority and revenues.
H7792.origine: The Aramaic word shur comes from the same-root Hebrew root (שׁוּר). This root denotes a raised and protective construction. In Hebrew, it is also found in words related to building and fortification. The wall is primarily a human work, a demonstration of strength and civil organization.
H7792.emploi: The word appears three times in Aramaic in Ezra 4:12-16, all in accusations made against the Jews by their adversaries. The context is political: the enemies of Jerusalem report to King Artaxerxes that the rebuilding of the walls threatens the established order and the subjugation of the Persian province. The wall is never described in isolation, but always as an act of rebellion or restoration of power. The Aramaic shur, the diplomatic language of the empire, underscores the administrative and military stakes of these walls.
H7792.portee: For the Christian reader, the walls of Jerusalem remind us that the restoration of God's people is a visible and public matter, which provokes resistance from the powers of the world. Ezra shows that rebuilding what God has allowed to be destroyed requires courage in the face of political opposition. It is a lesson on perseverance in God's work despite external obstacles.

sens: desert region southwest of Palestine, at or within the Egyptian border
Area that the Israelites crossed after passing through the Red Sea
H7793.detail: 1. Shur is a desert region located southwest of Palestine, near the boundary of Egyptian territory. It is an arid and difficult place to traverse, where water is scarce (Exodus 15:22 mentions that the Israelites found no water there after three days of travel). 2. It is the path that the Israelites took after miraculously crossing the Red Sea under Moses' leadership: they had to traverse this desert of Shur to reach the heart of the Sinai Peninsula (Exodus 15:22). The region also served as a natural boundary for the movements of the peoples of that time, such as the Amalekites and other nations that inhabited it (1 Samuel 15:7, 27:8).
H7793.origine: The name Shur literally means "wall" in Hebrew, probably because this mountainous or naturally fortified region formed a barrier between Egypt and the desert of the Sinai Peninsula. It is an ancient geographical name that designates a well-known area to the peoples of the Levant and the Egyptians.
H7793.emploi: Shur appears six times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in historical narratives. It is mentioned as a geographical landmark in the story of Abraham (Genesis 16:7, 20:1) and in that of his descendants (Genesis 25:18). It is primarily the desert of Shur that the Israelites cross after the Exodus (Exodus 15:22), a crucial moment when God tests the faith of the people by depriving them of water. Later, it serves as a territorial boundary in the accounts of Saul and David's military campaigns against the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15:7, 27:8), showing that it remained a strategic and dangerous area in the southwest Levant.
H7793.portee: Shur reminds the reader that the Exodus is not just a journey: it is a crossing of the desert that purifies and shapes faith. This arid place symbolizes the necessary trial before entering the Promised Land. For Abraham as well, it represents a moment of flight and trust in God in a hostile place.

sens: robust domestic animal, used for plowing fields and transporting loads
head of cattle, taken in a general sense as property and wealth
animal offered in sacrifice or consumed as food
creature symbolizing brute strength or obedience
image of a foolish or unperceptive man
H7794.detail:
1. The ox is the quintessential work animal in ancient agriculture. It was harnessed to the plow to till the fields, as shown in Isaiah 7:25, and used to transport loads, particularly in religious processions (2 Samuel 6:13 where oxen are brought during the transport of the ark).
2. In economic and social language, the ox represents tangible and valuable wealth. When Jacob lists his possessions in Genesis 32:5, he places the oxen first as a sign of prosperity. The laws of Deuteronomy 22:1-4 protect another's ox, showing its importance as personal property.
3. The law of Moses distinguishes the ox as an acceptable offering to God (Leviticus 9:4, Leviticus 9:18) and as permitted food (Deuteronomy 14:4). It is a sacrificial animal in worship, but also a common food for meals.
4. The ox embodies power and solidity. Ezekiel 1:10 uses an ox's face as a symbol of strength in his theophanic vision.
5. In contrast, the image of the ox can evoke ignorance or carelessness: Isaiah 1:3 reproaches Israel for not understanding, "the ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's crib, but Israel does not know me." Proverbs 7:22 compares the seduced man to an ox going to slaughter, unaware of the danger.
H7794.origine: The Hebrew word שׁוֹר (shor) comes from an ancient root denoting strength and vigor. It is attested in all ancient Semitic languages; Aramaic uses תּוֹר (tor) in the same sense. In Greek, the word βοῦς (bous) regularly translates שׁוֹר in the Septuagint. The ox was the fundamental work and wealth animal in Israel and the ancient Near East, hence its constant importance in biblical vocabulary.
H7794.emploi: The word שׁוֹר appears 69 times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in the sense of domestic work animal and wealth. It is particularly frequent in the laws of the Decalogue and Leviticus (Exodus 20:17 prohibits coveting a neighbor's ox; Exodus 21:28-36 regulates accidents involving oxen). Historical narratives mention it as a sign of prosperity or war booty (Joshua 7:24). The Psalms and biblical wisdom use it either literally (Proverbs 14:4: "No ox, no harvest"), or in moral and spiritual imagery (Psalms 106:20 where Israel exchanges its glory for the image of an ox that eats grass).
H7794.portee: The ox reminds the believer of God's providence toward His people and the importance of honest work in human life. The laws that protect another's ox teach justice and respect for others' property. The prophetic and sapiential images of the ox invite us to meditate on our spiritual responsibility: are we as aware of God as the ox is of its owner?

sens: A sequence of elements aligned on the same line
H7795.detail: 1. A row is a sequence of objects or plants arranged regularly one after the other on the same line. In Isaiah 28:25, the prophet describes a farmer who sows wheat "in rows": instead of scattering the seeds randomly, he places them in an orderly and spaced manner so that each plant has its own place. The image evokes the careful and intelligent work of the farmer who prepares his field.
H7795.origine: The Hebrew root suggests the idea of orderly placement, alignment. The word concretely designates what arranges or aligns naturally: a row of stones, a row of plants in a field. Although the exact meaning presents some uncertainties in ancient sources, the biblical usage in an agricultural context is clear.
H7795.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 28:25. This unique usage situates it in a description of the work of the intelligent farmer: God, or the one who follows Him, sows different crops "in rows" — that is, in a methodical and planned manner. The agricultural context suggests that the word describes a practice of organized sowing, which contrasts with random scattering.
H7795.portee: This passage reminds the believer that God acts with wisdom and order, and that human work itself should reflect this intelligence and planning. A row is not an accident: it is the fruit of intention, of know-how. This invites recognition of how God leads history and His kingdom with a precise purpose.

sens: Valley or intermittent watercourse in Palestine
Region where Delilah, the woman Samson loved, lived
H7796.detail: 1. Sorek is a valley (or wadi, meaning a watercourse that flows only during rains) located in Palestine. The name literally means "choice vine," suggesting a fertile region suitable for vine cultivation. 2. It is in this valley that Delilah lived, the woman with whom Samson had a romantic relationship and who ultimately betrayed him by revealing the secret of his strength (Judges 16:4).
H7796.origine: The Hebrew name Sorek means "choice vine" or "selected vine," evoking superior quality vines. It comes from a root related to excellence and selection. This meaning likely reflects the natural fertility and productivity of this valley in the Promised Land.
H7796.emploi: Sorek appears only once in the Bible, at the point where we learn that Samson loved a woman named Delilah who lived in the valley of Sorek (Judges 16:4). This context shows that Sorek was an inhabited place, well-known enough to be mentioned without further explanation. The valley was likely a fertile region of the Philistine territory, bordering Israel, which explains why Samson, an Israelite, could access it.

sens: Experience a lively and manifest joy
Find pleasure in something
Exult, celebrate with enthusiasm
Enjoy a deep satisfaction
H7797.detail:
1. To rejoice primarily means to experience intense and visible joy: it is to leap for joy, to exult. The horse that "rejoices in its strength" by leaping into battle (Job 39:24) clearly illustrates this physical, bodily expression of joy.
2. The word also designates finding pleasure or satisfaction in something, especially in what is good or just. The psalmist "rejoices in following your precepts" (Psalms 119:14): he tastes a deep joy in obeying God.
3. To rejoice can also mean to exult, to celebrate with éclat — not only for oneself but for others or for a cause. When the psalmist calls those who seek God to be in "joy" (Psalms 40:17), he invites to a joy that radiates and expresses itself.
4. Finally, it is to enjoy a moral or spiritual satisfaction: God Himself "takes pleasure" in blessing His people (Deuteronomy 28:63), and the young bride brings "joy" to her fiancé (Isaiah 62:5). This joy is agreement, contentment, complacency.
H7797.origine: The Hebrew verb שׂוּשׂ (sus) comes from a root that evokes the idea of leaping, jumping, or stirring with joy. It is from the same family as the word "joy" in Hebrew. The verb always depicts a joy that does not remain confined but is expressed through the body and visible emotion. This is why it opposes mere inner satisfaction: it is a joy that bursts forth.
H7797.emploi: The verb appears 24 times in the Old Testament, notably in the Psalms (where the believer rejoices in God) and among the prophets (where God or the people rejoice in fulfilled promises). It is used for the joy of the righteous who meditates on the Law (Psalms 119:14, 119:162), for the joy of the people (Isaiah 65:18-19), and even for God's joy in His people (Deuteronomy 30:9, Zephaniah 3:17: "The Lord your God rejoices over you"). Sometimes it designates malicious joy, such as that of the enemy who triumphs (Lamentations 1:21, Ezekiel 21:15). The context determines whether this joy is legitimate or condemnable.
H7797.portee: For the believer, this word teaches that joy before God is not a shameful emotion to hide: it is an act of trust that expresses itself. To rejoice in God is to affirm that He is good. Conversely, learning that God rejoices in us (Zephaniah 3:17) reveals that we are not merely tolerated but loved and celebrated by Him — a truth that transforms and liberates.

sens: secretary or scribe of King David
H7798.detail: Shavsha is the name of a high-ranking man during the reign of King David. He served as a royal secretary, managing the archives, correspondence, and official documents of the palace. In 1 Chronicles 18:16, he is mentioned alongside the priests Zadok and Abiathar, which shows the importance of his position in the administration of the kingdom. It is a position of trust that requires literacy and direct access to the king.
H7798.origine: The name Shavsha means "nobility" in Hebrew. This man is referred to by several variants of the same name in biblical accounts: Shavsha, Sheva, and Shisha according to the books and manuscripts. He is also another way of designating Seraiah (שְׂרָיָהוּ), another name by which this royal officer was known. These variants reflect the different transcriptions of the name in textual traditions.
H7798.emploi: Shavsha is mentioned only once in the Segond at the passage of 1 Chronicles 18:16, where he is identified as secretary to King David. He is part of David's administrative and religious team during the height of his reign. The same person appears elsewhere in the Bible under other forms of his name (Sheva in 2 Samuel 20:25, Shisha in 1 Kings 4:3), always in a high-ranking officer role. His sons, Elihoreph and Ahijah, also served in the royal administration, showing that this position was passed down in the family.

sens: White or colored flower, elegant and fragrant, growing from a bulb
Ornamental motif in the shape of a lily, used in the decoration of temples and buildings
Image of beauty, purity, and grace
Image of fragility or vulnerability before God
H7799.detail:
1. The lily is a real flower, known in the East for its beauty and brilliance; the Bible speaks of it as a plant endowed with natural grace, particularly admired for its appearance.
2. In royal and religious constructions, the lily becomes a motif for elaborate decoration: in Jerusalem, the columns of Solomon's temple and the large bronze basin were adorned with capitals and motifs in the shape of lilies (1 Kings 7:19, 7:26), symbolizing magnificence and royalty.
3. The lily most often appears as a poetic image of feminine beauty and tenderness: in the Song of Solomon, the beloved compares herself to a lily of the valleys (2:1), and the loving couple meets among the lilies, symbolizing a delightful and pure place.
4. In the prophets, the lily also expresses the fragility of human beauty before God, who can destroy or restore it according to His will, as in Hosea 14:5 where God promises that His people will flourish like the lily.
H7799.origine: The Hebrew word *shushan* refers to the lily flower, probably the white lily of the Mediterranean, widely found in the ancient East. The term is likely of Persian or Egyptian origin, brought to the Levant through trade. It does not have a common Hebrew root and mainly appears in poetic and architectural contexts. In Greek, it is translated as *krinon*, retaining the same botanical reference.
H7799.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in two distinct contexts: first in the description of the religious architecture of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 7:19, 7:22, 7:26; 2 Chronicles 4:5), where lilies adorn the columns and vessels, emblematic of royal and divine beauty. Secondly, it appears abundantly in the romantic poetry of the Song of Solomon (2:1, 2:2, 2:16, 4:5, 5:13, 6:2, 6:3, 7:3), where the lily symbolizes the beauty and grace of the beloved. The word also appears in the titles of the Psalms (45:1, 60:1, 69:1, 80:1), probably as a melodic or liturgical indication. A prophetic occurrence in Hosea 14:5 reminds that the beauty of the lily reflects that which God grants to His restored people.
H7799.portee: The lily teaches the reader that true beauty — the kind celebrated in Scripture — is not the result of human effort, but a gift of divine creation. By contemplating the lily, one learns not to overly concern oneself with appearance, but to trust in God who adorns the flowers with glory. For lovers reading the Song of Solomon, the lily reminds that purified human love, aligned with God, rises to share in the beauty of divine creation.

sens: Make a U-turn, go back to the starting point
Abandon a direction, a path, a wrong conduct
Return to God after having strayed; repent
Turn away from God or His justice (referring to God or man)
Restore, bring something back to its previous state
Give back, restore, reestablish
H7725O.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to make a U-turn, to return from where one came. When Israel refuses to return to God after His punishments, God asks the prophet to assess whether they will "return" (Nehemiah 9:26).
2. The verb also expresses the idea of changing path or direction. Jeremiah cries out to the people: "Let each of you return from your evil way, amend your actions" (Jeremiah 35:15), meaning: leave the path of evil.
3. Applied to the relationship with God, "return" means to repent: to acknowledge one's sin and turn back to God. This is the heart of the prophets' message.
4. The word can also express the opposite movement: turning away from God (apostasy) or turning away from justice. Ezekiel asks: "If the righteous turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity... he shall die" (Ezekiel 18:24).
5. The verb also carries the idea of bringing back, restoring, reestablishing: God can "bring back" His people to Him after exile (Isaiah 59:20).
6. In commands or requests, "return" can mean to give back, restore, reestablish something to its original state.
H7725O.origine: The Hebrew word shuv is a very ancient and common root in Semitic languages, primarily meaning physical movement: to turn, to make a U-turn. The basic image is that of the body turning around or the path being abandoned. Like many movement verbs in Hebrew, shuv quickly acquires a figurative and spiritual meaning: to change moral or religious direction. In the Greek translations of the Old Testament, it is often rendered by Greek words meaning "turn" or "return," which has influenced the vocabulary of repentance in the New Testament.
H7725O.emploi: The verb return is extremely frequent in the Hebrew Bible (77 occurrences provided), especially in the prophetic books: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel. It primarily denotes physical return (return from exile, return to the land), but its spiritual usage predominates: it is the constant call of the prophets to Israel to repent and return to the Covenant with God. The opposite movement also appears: apostasy, when Israel turns away from God (Ezekiel 18:24). In judicial or administrative contexts, the verb means to give back, restore, reestablish. Each major prophet uses it, particularly in scenes of national or personal repentance.
H7725O.portee: This word is at the heart of the prophetic message: it reminds the Christian that returning to God is possible; it is indeed the constant call of His heart. Repentance is not a definitive humiliation but a joyful U-turn towards the One who awaits the return of His children. Ezekiel states it emphatically: "I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but rather that he turn from his way and live" (Ezekiel 33:11). It is also a warning: one can also turn away from justice, which calls for vigilance.

sens: physically place an object
establish a decision or order
transform into something
neglect or ignore (consider as of little importance)
take to heart, attach importance to
H7761H.detail:
1. Physically place an object in a location: to put in position. Example: one puts a stone over the opening of a pit (Daniel 6:17).
2. Establish a decision or order, decree, fix something. Example: the hewn stones are laid in the walls to build the temple (Ezra 5:8).
3. Reduce to a given state or condition, transform. Example: to put into pieces, reduce to a heap of rubbish (Daniel 2:5).
4. Neglect, ignore, consider as of little importance, regard as worthless. Example: the three young men pay no attention to the king and his gods (Daniel 3:12), Daniel paid no attention to the king's decree (Daniel 6:13).
5. Pay attention to something, take to heart, make it one's concern. Example: the king took to heart to deliver Daniel and sought to save him (Daniel 6:14).
H7761H.origine: The Aramaic verb שׂוּם (sum) has the fundamental meaning of "to place" or "to put in position." Its etymology refers to the idea of placing something in a specific location. In biblical Hebrew, the corresponding verb is שׂוּם (sûm), attested many times with the same semantic field. The word can also express the action of fixing, decreeing, or establishing an order, and by extension, to take into account or to despise something.
H7761H.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears 6 times in the provided passages, exclusively in the book of Daniel and in Ezra, the only Aramaic portions of the Old Testament. The usage is varied: first concrete (putting a stone), then decreeing (to lay, to establish), and then figurative (neglecting, ignoring, taking to heart). The contexts reveal the stakes of the captives: the reconstruction of the temple (Ezra 5:8), the pressure from King Nebuchadnezzar threatening the Chaldeans (Daniel 2:5), the civic disobedience of the three young men and Daniel towards royal orders (Daniel 3:12, 6:13), and the personal concern of the king for Daniel (Daniel 6:14). The word shows how authorities impose their will and how the faithful refuse to bend.
H7761H.portee: This verb sheds light on a central theme of Daniel: the tension between obedience to God and submission to a pagan king. When the young men or Daniel "pay no attention" to the king, they affirm a hierarchy of loyalties. Conversely, when the king "takes to heart" Daniel's fate, he acknowledges a value that his own law would have destroyed. The reader discovers that certain human orders do not deserve consideration in light of God's commandments, and that even the hearts of kings can be touched by faithfulness.

sens: Put in place, install someone in a function or position
Fix, determine, decree something
Place, lay or install something
H7761I.detail:
1. Establish someone in a function: give a person a role, an official mission, or a responsibility. Cyrus the Persian "established" Sheshbazzar as governor (Ezra 5:14), meaning he appointed and installed him in that position with the authority that comes with it.
2. Fix or decree: definitively settle a decision, a law, or a rule. This means to lay something down in a stable and durable way, which cannot be easily modified.
3. Place or lay: materially arrange an object in a location, install it in such a way that it holds or is in place.
H7761I.origine: The Aramaic verb שׂוּם (sum) comes from an ancient Semitic root meaning "to place, to lay." This verb expresses the idea of putting something or someone in a given location, or giving them a position, a defined place. It is found in biblical Aramaic with nuances ranging from material placement to formal investiture. The root is related to Hebrew verbs of similar meaning, although in Hebrew other more common forms are used.
H7761I.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears only once in the Bible in Ezra 5:14, in the context of the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem. King Cyrus, after returning the sacred objects taken from Jerusalem, entrusts their transport to Sheshbazzar by appointing him governor. The verb "establish" here describes an official act of appointment and placement of authority. This term reflects the Persian administrative practice of appointing provincial governors in the empire.
H7761I.portee: This verb reminds us that human authorities act only within the limits set by God. Cyrus, despite his power, only "establishes" Sheshbazzar according to the divine plan for the restoration of the temple. This encourages the believer to recognize that even earthly political powers are instruments of God's will to fulfill His promises.

sens: edible white bulb, pungent flavor
food appreciated in ancient Egypt
H7762.detail:
1. Garlic is a white bulb that can be eaten cooked or raw, with a strong and pungent flavor. In Numbers 11:5, the Israelites in the desert long for the garlic they ate in Egypt, where this vegetable was abundant and part of their daily diet.
2. Garlic here appears as a symbol of the former life in Egypt: the people, tired of the manna in the desert, nostalgically remember the varied and flavorful dishes of their former country. This concrete food becomes a sign of all the earthly pleasures they have abandoned.
H7762.origine: The Hebrew word שׁוּם comes from a root that designates the bulb. Garlic was known and cultivated throughout the ancient Mediterranean and Middle Eastern world. It is a simple garden plant, with no deep etymological connection: the word directly names the object.
H7762.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 11:5. The Israelites, having recently come out of Egypt, complain to the Lord and list what they miss from their previous life. Garlic is included in a list of various Egyptian foods—fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions—that contrast with the monotony of the manna. This passage shows how much the Israelites regretted the earthly flavors and forgot the wonders that God was doing for them.
H7762.portee: This simple word reminds us of the temptation to idealize the past and forget what God is doing for us. Eating garlic in Egypt was an ordinary pleasure; but for the Israelites in the desert, this memory becomes a temptation to turn away from the Lord who nourishes them. It is a lesson on ingratitude and the power of worldly habits.

sens: Servant of King Joash of Judah, father of Jozabad
Moabite man during the divided monarchy
H7763G.detail:
1. Shomer is the father of Jozabad, one of the two servants who assassinated King Joash of Judah (2 Kings 12:21). He is identified as a Moabite, meaning he was from Moab, the neighboring country east of the Jordan.
2. His name means "guardian" or "one who guards" in Hebrew, but there is nothing in the text that tells us he held a guarding function. It is simply a family name passed down to his descendants.
H7763G.origine: The name Shomer comes from the Hebrew root that means "to guard," "to observe," "to watch." This same root has given rise to other biblical names like Shimrith, which is a feminine name from the same family (mentioned in 2 Chronicles 24:26 to designate the mother of Jozabad). The name expresses the idea of vigilance and protection, qualities expected of a guardian.
H7763G.emploi: Shomer appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 12:21, where he is mentioned as the father of Jozabad. This Jozabad is one of the two servants who conspired against King Joash and assassinated him. The context shows that Shomer was a man of servile condition, since his son served at the king's court. Although he is identified as a Moabite, this apparently did not prevent his family from integrating into Jewish life and serving the king.
